lessons.title: DNS steering and resilient discovery
lessons.summary: Use DNS for coarse routing while recognising resolver geography, health and dependency limits.
lessons.body:
Once record types and expiry are clear, DNS becomes a routing layer. It is best suited to choosing a region or data centre; use per-connection or per-request balancing inside the destination.

## DNS as a load-balancing tool

The authoritative server decides what to return, and it can be clever about it.

### Round-robin DNS

Return several `A` records and rotate their order:

Illustrative zone-file fragment, not a complete zone:

```dns
; One name publishes three backend IPs.
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.10
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.11
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.12
```

Clients usually try the first, so load spreads roughly evenly. (Not always: some operating systems sort addresses using RFC 6724 rules, which can undo the rotation and favour one IP.) It's simple, but crude:

- **No health awareness.** Plain DNS keeps handing out a dead server's IP.
- **Uneven.** One big corporate resolver may send thousands of users to the same IP.
- **Slow to react,** because of caching.

### Smarter answers

Managed DNS services (Route 53, Azure Traffic Manager, NS1, Cloudflare) layer policies on top:

- **Health-checked failover:** stop returning an IP when its health check fails.
- **Weighted:** choose DNS answers with 90:10 relative weights for a `v1`/`v2` canary. Resolver caching and connection reuse mean request traffic need not follow those exact percentages.
- **Geo / latency-based:** return the region nearest the user (covered in the global traffic lesson).

The resolver, not the user, is what the authoritative server sees. If a user in Paris uses a resolver in Virginia, they may be sent to a US region. The **EDNS Client Subnet** extension lets resolvers pass along part of the client's IP (for example a /24) to fix this, at some cost to privacy and cache efficiency.

> [!tip] Where DNS load balancing fits
> DNS is great for coarse, global decisions: which region, which data centre. Inside a data centre, use a real load balancer, which reacts in seconds and balances per connection or per request.

## DNS as a single point of failure

If your authoritative DNS is unreachable, clients without usable cached or serve-stale answers cannot resolve your names, even if every server is healthy. In October 2016, a DDoS on Dyn made Twitter, GitHub, Netflix and others unreachable for many users.

Mitigations:

- Use a provider with a large **anycast** network.
- Consider **two independent DNS providers** (both listed in your `NS` records).
- Don't set TTLs so low that a short DNS outage immediately becomes a full outage.

## Inside your own systems

DNS is also the default service-discovery mechanism inside clusters. In Kubernetes, a normal `orders.prod.svc.cluster.local` Service resolves to a stable virtual IP; routing updates behind it handle changing Pods without a DNS change. Headless Services instead return Pod addresses, so DNS caching matters directly. Long-lived connections can stay attached to an existing backend in either case.

## Key takeaways

- Plain round-robin DNS lacks backend health awareness and can distribute traffic unevenly.
- Geo steering commonly sees the recursive resolver; EDNS Client Subnet improves the signal with privacy and cache costs.
- Independent authoritative providers can reduce a DNS-provider failure risk; Kubernetes discovery still interacts with long-lived connections.

## Further reading

- [Choosing a routing policy (Amazon Route 53)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy.html)
- [Client subnet in DNS queries (RFC 7871)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7871)
- [DNS for Services and Pods (Kubernetes)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/)

questions.prompt: You use plain round-robin DNS with three `A` records for `api.example.com`. One server dies. What happens?

options.text: DNS automatically stops returning the dead IP
options.explanation: Plain DNS has no idea whether a server is alive. Health-checked DNS (e.g. Route 53 failover) can do this, but plain round robin keeps returning all three records.

options.text: All traffic fails because DNS needs every server healthy
options.explanation: DNS doesn't check servers at all. Clients given one of the two live IPs succeed normally.

options.text: Traffic is automatically spread over the two remaining servers with no errors
options.explanation: That's what a load balancer with health checks does. DNS round robin has no feedback loop, so errors continue until the record is removed and caches expire.

options.text: Roughly a third of new connection attempts hit the dead IP, and clients that don't retry another address fail until the record is changed and caches expire
options.explanation: Correct. Each resolver keeps handing out the dead IP. Some clients (browsers) try the next address after a timeout; many API clients don't, so they fail.

questions.workedExample:
1. Resolvers return all three IPs in rotating order, and many clients simply try the first one.
2. With one server dead, the dead IP comes first in roughly one lookup in three, so about a third of new connection attempts try it first.
3. Plain DNS has no health checks, so it keeps handing out the dead IP until someone removes the record, and then caches keep the old set until their TTLs expire.
4. Browsers usually fall back to the next address after a timeout (often seconds); many HTTP libraries just fail.

That is why DNS is used for coarse routing, with a health-checking load balancer behind each address.

questions.prompt: You use geo-based DNS to send European users to `eu-west` and US users to `us-east`. Analytics show many users in Germany are being routed to `us-east`. They all use a large public resolver. What's the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: German ISPs block European IP ranges
options.explanation: There's no such blocking. The users aren't failing to reach Europe; DNS is choosing the wrong region for them.

options.text: The `A` record TTL is too long
options.explanation: A long TTL slows changes, but it doesn't cause the wrong region to be chosen in the first place. The selection uses the resolver's location.

options.text: The public resolver's query reaches your authoritative server from a US-located IP, so geo-DNS sees the resolver's location. Support EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) so you see the client's subnet.
options.explanation: Correct. Authoritative servers only see the resolver's address. ECS lets the resolver include a truncated client subnet, so the geo decision uses the user's real network.

options.text: Geo-DNS only works with IPv6
options.explanation: Geo-DNS works on IPv4 and IPv6 equally. The problem is whose IP the geolocation is based on.

questions.workedExample:
1. Geo-DNS decides based on **the IP that sent the query**, which is the recursive resolver, not the user.
2. If the resolver's egress appears to be in the US (or its anycast routing lands the query at a US site), users get the US answer.
3. **ECS** adds e.g. the client's /24 to the query, so the authoritative server can geolocate the user.
4. Trade-offs: ECS leaks some client information and fragments resolver caches (one entry per subnet), so not every resolver sends it.
5. Alternative fix: anycast at the network layer, which routes by where the user's packets actually enter.

questions.prompt: You're designing DNS for a service that must stay reachable even if your DNS provider suffers a large DDoS like the 2016 Dyn attack. Which approach most directly addresses that risk?

options.text: Lower all TTLs to 5 seconds so you can react faster
options.explanation: This makes things worse: when the provider is down, caches expire within seconds and every client immediately fails to resolve. Longer TTLs actually ride out short DNS outages.

options.text: Host the zone on two independent authoritative providers and list both sets of name servers in your `NS` records
options.explanation: Correct. Resolvers try the other `NS` set if one doesn't answer, so an attack on one provider doesn't take you offline. You must keep the zones in sync (via zone transfers or automation).

options.text: Put the website behind a CDN
options.explanation: A CDN protects your origin servers, but users still need DNS to find the CDN. If the DNS provider is down, they can't resolve the name at all.

options.text: Use DNS over HTTPS
options.explanation: DoH protects the privacy of the client–resolver hop. It does nothing if the authoritative servers can't answer.

questions.workedExample:
1. The failure is: **authoritative servers unreachable**.
2. Once cached records expire, clients without usable serve-stale data cannot resolve the name, however healthy your servers are.
3. Redundancy at that layer means **multiple providers**: e.g. `NS` records for both `ns1.provider-a.net` and `ns1.provider-b.net`.
4. Supporting moves: moderate TTLs (minutes to hours for stable records) so caches bridge short outages.
5. Cost: keeping two providers' zones in sync, and advanced features (geo, health checks) may differ between them.

lessons.title: TCP windows and slow start
lessons.summary: Explain why a new connection needs several round trips to deliver even a modest response on a fast link.
lessons.body:
Transport performance is about how much data may be in flight, not only raw bandwidth. This unit shows why a brand-new connection is slow even on a fast link.

Every HTTP request rides on a transport protocol. The choice of transport, and how HTTP uses it, explains most of the performance differences between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. These short units build up from TCP and UDP to the problem each HTTP version was designed to fix.

## TCP: a reliable, ordered byte stream

TCP gives applications the illusion of a reliable pipe:

- **Connection-oriented:** a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) costs 1 RTT before data flows.
- **Reliable:** lost segments are detected and retransmitted.
- **Ordered:** bytes are delivered to the app in the order they were sent.
- **Flow control:** the receiver advertises how much it can buffer.
- **Congestion control:** the sender probes for available bandwidth.

That last point matters for performance. A new TCP connection starts in **slow start**, with a small congestion window: commonly 10 segments, about 14 KB (proposed by the Experimental RFC 6928; the actual initial window depends on the implementation and configuration). The window roughly doubles each round trip until loss appears, after which the sender cuts it (by half for classic Reno, by about 30% for CUBIC, the Linux default) and grows more cautiously.

In an idealised model (no loss, immediate acknowledgements, a 14 KB start that doubles every round trip) the amount a fresh connection can deliver grows like this:

| Round trip | Window | Total delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14 KB | 14 KB |
| 2 | 28 KB | 42 KB |
| 3 | 56 KB | 98 KB |
| 4 | 112 KB | 210 KB |

So a 200 KB response needs about four round trips on a new connection, whatever the link speed. That separates two costs that are easy to blur:

```formula essential
T ≈ k × RTT + 8S / B
where
T: the time to deliver a response after the request is sent, in seconds (s)
k: the number of round trips the sender needs; set by the congestion window, so 1 on a warm connection whose window already fits the response and several on a new one
RTT: the round-trip time, in seconds (s)
S: the response size, in bytes
8: the number of bits in a byte
B: the link bandwidth, in bits per second (bit/s)
≈: approximately equal to (a simplified model that ignores loss and processing)
In words: delivery time has a round-trip part and a wire part. For a small or medium response on a new connection the round-trip part dominates, so a faster link barely helps while fewer round trips help a lot.
```

For example, on a 1 Gbps link a 200 KB response needs under 2 ms of wire time, but at a 50 ms RTT the four slow-start rounds take about 200 ms. Upgrading the link would shave a millisecond; reusing a warm connection, whose window has already grown, would deliver it in about one round trip.

**Warm, reused connections are fast; new ones are slow.** This is why connection pooling and keep-alive matter so much between services as well as for browsers.

> [!note] TCP Fast Open
> TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413) lets a returning client put data in the SYN, saving the handshake RTT. Deployment depends on both endpoints and middlebox compatibility.

## Key takeaways

- TCP provides reliability, ordering, flow control and congestion control.
- A fresh connection’s small window can dominate a response even on a fast link.
- Bandwidth shortens the wire part only; reuse avoids repeated setup and window growth. The doubling model assumes no loss and simplified ACK timing.

## Further reading

- [Increasing TCP’s initial window (RFC 6928)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6928)
- [Building blocks of TCP (High Performance Browser Networking)](https://hpbn.co/building-blocks-of-tcp/)

questions.prompt: Service A calls service B for every user request, opening a **new** TCP + TLS 1.3 connection each time. Responses are about 60 KB, the RTT is 30 ms and the network is 10 Gbps. Profiling shows each call takes about five round trips. What explains this, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The 10 Gbps link is saturated; upgrade to 25 Gbps
options.explanation: Moving 60 KB takes well under a millisecond at 10 Gbps. The round-trip count, not bandwidth, is the cost, and a faster link does not reduce it.

options.text: B is slow to process requests; add more B instances
options.explanation: Server time would not show up as a fixed number of network round trips. The pattern matches connection setup plus slow start.

options.text: TLS 1.3 needs four round trips; downgrade to TLS 1.2
options.explanation: A full TLS 1.3 handshake needs one round trip, and TLS 1.2 needs two, so downgrading would add a trip.

options.text: Two round trips go on the TCP and TLS handshakes, and a fresh connection's small window needs about three more rounds to deliver 60 KB; pool and reuse connections so most calls take about one round trip
options.explanation: Correct. A new connection pays setup and starts with a window of about 14 KB that roughly doubles each round trip (14, then 28, then 56 KB). A warm pooled connection has no setup and a grown window, so it can send the whole response in about one round.

questions.workedExample:
Count where the round trips go on a fresh connection:

| Step | Round trips |
|---|---|
| TCP handshake | 1 |
| TLS 1.3 handshake | 1 |
| Data: first 14 KB window | 1 |
| Data: next 28 KB | 1 |
| Data: next 56 KB (covers the rest) | 1 |

That is about five round trips, matching the profile. (The request itself goes out with the first data round.)

None of those trips gets shorter with more bandwidth. A pooled connection skips the two setup trips and already has a large window, so the same call takes roughly one round trip: about five times faster in this simplified, loss-free model.

questions.prompt: On a brand-new connection, a 90 KB response is delivered with a congestion window that starts at about 14 KB and doubles each round trip. The RTT is 100 ms and the link is 1 Gbps; there is no loss. The team proposes upgrading to 10 Gbps to speed this response up. Predict the effect.

options.text: About 10 times faster, because the link is 10 times faster
options.explanation: That assumes the wire is the bottleneck. At 1 Gbps the 90 KB already takes under a millisecond on the wire; the time goes on round trips while the window grows.

options.text: About 10 times faster, because slow start doubles faster on a faster link
options.explanation: The window grows per round trip, as acknowledgements come back, not per unit of bandwidth. A faster link does not shorten the round trip.

options.text: Almost no change: delivery needs about three round trips of window growth (14, 42, then 98 KB delivered in total), roughly 300 ms, and the link speed barely affects that
options.explanation: Correct. On a new connection the round-trip part dominates for a response this size. Reusing a warm connection, or a shorter RTT, would help; extra bandwidth would not.

options.text: It becomes slower, because more bandwidth triggers more loss
options.explanation: A faster link does not cause loss by itself. The change is simply irrelevant to the dominant cost.

questions.workedExample:
Track how much a fresh connection has delivered after each round trip in this idealised model:

| Round trip | Window | Total delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14 KB | 14 KB |
| 2 | 28 KB | 42 KB |
| 3 | 56 KB | 98 KB |

1. Two rounds deliver only 42 KB, so a 90 KB response needs a third: about three 100 ms round trips.
2. The wire time for 90 KB at 1 Gbps is already under a millisecond; at 10 Gbps it is even smaller, but it was never the bottleneck.
3. Delivery time has a round-trip part and a wire part. Here the round-trip part is hundreds of times larger, so only fewer or shorter round trips help: a reused connection with a grown window, or a server closer to the user.

lessons.title: Datagrams and HTTP/1.1 concurrency
lessons.summary: Choose datagrams for disposable updates and explain HTTP/1.1’s parallel-connection workarounds.
lessons.body:
Transport ordering is useful when every byte matters, but can hurt when a newer update replaces an old one. HTTP/1.1 has a separate concurrency problem: responses on each connection remain ordered.

## UDP: just datagrams

UDP is almost nothing on top of IP:

- No handshake, no connection state.
- No retransmission, no ordering, no congestion control.
- Each datagram is independent; it may be lost, duplicated or reordered.

That sounds worse, but it's exactly what some applications want:

| Use | Why UDP |
|---|---|
| DNS | One packet each way; retry is cheap |
| Voice/video calls | A late packet is useless; skip it |
| Games | Latest state matters, not old state |
| QUIC (HTTP/3) | Builds its own reliability in user space |

> [!note] Reliability isn't free
> TCP's ordering guarantee means one lost packet holds back everything after it, even data that arrived fine. That's **head-of-line (HOL) blocking** at the transport layer, and it's the thread that ties this whole lesson together.

## HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection

HTTP/1.1 (first specified in 1997, now RFC 9112) made **persistent connections** (`keep-alive`), so one TCP connection can carry many requests in sequence. But on each connection, a response must finish before the next request's response can start:

```
Conn 1: [req A ][resp A    ][req B][resp B]
Conn 2: [req C ][resp C][req D ][resp D   ]
...up to ~6 connections per origin
```

This is **HTTP-level head-of-line blocking**: a slow response blocks everything queued behind it on that connection. *Pipelining* (sending several requests without waiting) was specified but never worked reliably because responses still had to come back in order, and buggy proxies broke it. Browsers turned it off.

Workarounds from the HTTP/1.1 era:

- Browsers open **~6 parallel connections** per origin.
- Sites used **domain sharding** (`img1.`, `img2.`...) to get more connections.
- **Spriting and concatenation** bundled many small files into one.

All of these add handshakes, slow-start penalties or cache-busting problems.

## Key takeaways

- UDP supplies independent datagrams without TCP’s reliability or ordering.
- For frequent position updates, a newer state can be more useful than recovering a stale packet.
- HTTP/1.1 reuses connections but ordered responses limit concurrency on each connection.

## Further reading

- [User Datagram Protocol (RFC 768)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768)
- [HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
- [HTTP/1.x (High Performance Browser Networking)](https://hpbn.co/http1x/)

questions.prompt: You're building a multiplayer game that sends each player's position 30 times a second. Why do many such games use UDP rather than TCP for position updates?

options.text: UDP encrypts packets automatically
options.explanation: UDP has no encryption at all. Encryption comes from a layer on top (DTLS, QUIC or the game's own scheme).

options.text: UDP guarantees delivery faster than TCP
options.explanation: UDP guarantees nothing about delivery. It's attractive precisely because it doesn't try to deliver everything.

options.text: TCP can't send more than one message per second
options.explanation: TCP can carry very high message rates. The issue isn't throughput but head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.

options.text: A lost update is superseded 33 ms later, so retransmitting it (and blocking newer updates behind it, as TCP would) only adds lag
options.explanation: Correct. TCP's in-order delivery would hold back fresh positions until a stale one is retransmitted. UDP lets the game drop the stale packet and use the newest state.

questions.workedExample:
1. At 30 updates per second, a fresh position arrives roughly every 33 ms, and each one replaces the last.
2. With TCP, if one packet is lost, loss detection and retransmission take time, say tens of milliseconds. Meanwhile the next updates arrive, but TCP **can't deliver them** until the lost one is filled in, because it delivers bytes strictly in order.
3. Result: a visible stutter, all to deliver a position that is already out of date.
4. With UDP, the game simply uses the newest packet it has. Events that must not be lost (a kill, a purchase) can be sent with the game's own lightweight acknowledgements.

questions.prompt: In HTTP/1.1, why did browsers open about six TCP connections per origin?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 closes the connection after every request
options.explanation: HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default (keep-alive). The limit is concurrency on a connection, not reuse.

options.text: Without HTTP/1.1 pipelining, each connection handles one request/response at a time, so parallel fetching needs more connections
options.explanation: Correct. Without working pipelining, a connection waits for each response to finish before the next can be sent; multiple connections are the only way to fetch resources concurrently.

options.text: Servers limited each connection to 100 KB
options.explanation: There's no such per-connection size limit in HTTP/1.1. Connections can carry arbitrarily large responses.

options.text: To provide redundancy in case one TCP connection drops
options.explanation: Redundancy isn't the reason. The six connections are for parallel fetching to work around HTTP-level head-of-line blocking.

questions.workedExample:
1. A page needs, say, 60 resources.
2. Without working pipelining, one HTTP/1.1 connection carries one request and response at a time, so each resource waits at least one round trip behind the previous one.
3. Six connections let six requests be in flight at once, cutting that queue roughly six-fold, at the price of five extra handshakes and five separate slow starts.

HTTP/2 removes the reason: it can carry many concurrent requests on one connection, subject to stream limits and flow control. Completion time still depends on response size, server work, congestion and loss.

lessons.title: HTTP/2 streams and backend pools
lessons.summary: Explain multiplexing, shared TCP loss and why persistent gRPC connections can skew L4 balancing.
lessons.body:
HTTP/2 solves HTTP/1.1’s response-order bottleneck by separating logical streams. It still shares TCP’s byte ordering and congestion window, and reused backend connections require appropriate balancing.

## HTTP/2: multiplexing over one connection

HTTP/2 (2015, now RFC 9113) keeps HTTP's semantics (methods, headers, status codes) but changes the wire format:

- **Binary framing.** Messages are split into frames.
- **Streams.** Each request/response is a stream with an ID; frames from many streams interleave on **one TCP connection**.
- **HPACK header compression.** Repeated headers (cookies, user agents) are sent as small table references.
- **Prioritisation** hints. The original dependency-tree scheme was complex and inconsistently implemented, and RFC 9113 deprecated it in favour of the simpler *Extensible Priorities* scheme (RFC 9218), which HTTP/3 also uses.

```
One TCP connection:
[A1][B1][C1][A2][C2][B2][A3]...
 A, B, C: streams, interleaved
```

A slow response no longer blocks fast ones, so the HTTP-level HOL problem is solved. The 6-connection limit, sharding and spriting become unnecessary, and often harmful (sharding defeats the single-connection design).

**Server push** was also part of HTTP/2, but it was hard to use well and browsers (Chrome in 2022) removed support. `103 Early Hints` is the replacement.

### The problem HTTP/2 can't fix

All those streams share one TCP byte stream. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back **every byte after it** until the retransmission arrives, even bytes belonging to unrelated streams:

```
Packets: [A1][B1][xx][A2][C2]
               lost ^
TCP delivers A1, B1, then WAITS.
A2 and C2 arrived but are stuck.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One shared parcel conveyor
> Several shoppers' items travel to the packing bench on one conveyor belt, in the order they were scanned. If one item falls off and has to be fetched again, the belt stops, so every shopper waits, even those whose items are already sitting on the belt.
>
> **How it maps:** the shoppers are HTTP/2 streams and the single belt is the one TCP connection, which hands bytes to the application strictly in order. The fallen item is a lost packet, and stopping the belt until it is replaced is TCP head-of-line blocking across unrelated streams.
>
> **Where it stops:** TCP does not physically halt the network; later packets still arrive and wait in the receiver's buffer, and the sender also slows down because of congestion control. HTTP/2 does solve the separate problem of one slow *response* holding up others.

On a clean network this rarely matters. On lossy mobile or Wi-Fi links (a few per cent loss), HTTP/2 over one connection can perform *worse* than HTTP/1.1 over six, for two reasons:

- A single loss stalls every stream instead of one-sixth of the traffic.
- The one connection's congestion window shrinks on loss, cutting throughput for everything. With six connections, only one window shrinks at a time.

## Connection reuse in back-end systems

These lessons apply between your own services too:

- **Pool connections.** Opening a new TCP+TLS connection per request to a database or downstream API adds 2+ RTTs and slow start every time. Keep-alive pools are essential.
- **HTTP/2 between services** (gRPC uses it) gives multiplexing over few connections. But a few long-lived connections can **unbalance an L4 load balancer**, which balances connections, not requests. Use an L7 balancer or client-side balancing.
- **Set a max connection age** so pools pick up DNS changes and spread across new backends.

> [!example] A real migration
> Google’s 2017 QUIC deployment paper reports benefits for Search and YouTube in its measured environment. That historical Google QUIC implementation predates standard IETF QUIC; its results are not a guaranteed HTTP/3 speed-up.
>
> Evidence gap: no reproducible benchmark for this app or your network is provided. Exact performance gains and CPU comparisons are omitted; measure representative workloads.

## Key takeaways

- HTTP/2 interleaves request streams and compresses headers on one TCP connection.
- TCP still holds back later bytes after a loss, so unrelated HTTP/2 streams can stall together.
- Long-lived HTTP/2 connections can pin work behind L4 balancing; L7 or client-side balancing distributes requests.

## Further reading

- [HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113)
- [HTTP/2 (High Performance Browser Networking)](https://hpbn.co/http2/)
- [Supported load balancers (Envoy)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancers)

questions.prompt: After moving from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2, your site is faster on office broadband but *slower* for users on a congested mobile network with ~2% packet loss. What best explains this?

options.text: All streams share one TCP connection, so each lost packet stalls every stream until it's retransmitted; with HTTP/1.1, a loss stalled only one of six connections
options.explanation: Correct. This is TCP-level head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 concentrates everything on one connection, so loss has a bigger blast radius, and every loss shrinks the congestion window that all traffic shares, instead of one of six.

options.text: HTTP/2's binary framing is harder for phones to parse
options.explanation: Binary framing alone does not explain a slowdown specifically correlated with packet loss. No CPU parsing benchmark is supplied; shared TCP ordering and congestion provide the relevant mechanism.

options.text: HPACK compression fails on mobile networks
options.explanation: HPACK works the same on any network. It saves bytes everywhere; it doesn't make loss worse.

options.text: Mobile networks don't support HTTP/2
options.explanation: HTTP/2 can use the same HTTPS-over-TCP path as HTTP/1.1. The observed loss-related slowdown has an explanation in shared TCP ordering; it does not establish a compatibility failure. Offered ALPN identifiers in a visible ClientHello can still reveal protocol preferences.

questions.workedExample:
1. HTTP/2 = many streams, **one** TCP connection.
2. TCP delivers bytes in order. If one packet is lost, every later packet waits in the receiver's buffer even if it belongs to another stream.
3. With about 2% loss and around a hundred packets in flight per round trip, most round trips contain at least one loss (roughly 87% in an idealised model with independent losses), so shared stalls happen constantly. Real losses can be correlated.
4. TCP also cuts its congestion window on loss (by half for Reno, about 30% for CUBIC). With one connection, *all* throughput drops; with six, only one connection's share does.
5. HTTP/3 fixes the cross-stream stall with per-stream loss recovery in QUIC.

questions.prompt: Your gRPC clients (HTTP/2) talk to 10 server pods behind an L4 (TCP) load balancer. After a scale-up from 10 to 20 pods, the new pods pass their health checks but sit idle while clients continue using their pre-scale-up, long-lived connections to the old pods. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: gRPC doesn't support more than 10 servers
options.explanation: gRPC has no such limit. The issue is how connections and requests are distributed, not a server count cap.

options.text: The new pods failed their health checks
options.explanation: The question states that the new pods pass their health checks. The remaining issue is that existing TCP connections stay pinned to the old backends.

options.text: The L4 balancer balances TCP connections, and each client multiplexes all its requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection made before scale-up. Use L7 (per-request) balancing or client-side balancing, and/or a max connection age.
options.explanation: Correct. An L4 balancer only decides when a connection opens. Existing connections stay pinned to old pods. L7 proxies (Envoy) or client-side balancing spread individual requests; a max connection age forces periodic reconnection.

options.text: HTTP/2 header compression routes requests to the same server
options.explanation: HPACK compresses headers within a connection; it has no role in choosing servers.

questions.workedExample:
1. L4 load balancing chooses a backend **per TCP connection**.
2. HTTP/2 clients open a connection once and send thousands of requests over it for hours.
3. Scale-up adds pods, but no client opens a new connection, so the new pods get nothing.
4. Fixes:
  - **L7 balancing** (Envoy, Linkerd, an ALB with gRPC support): balance each request (stream).
  - **Client-side balancing**: the gRPC client resolves all pod IPs and round-robins.
  - **`MAX_CONNECTION_AGE`** on the server: e.g. close after 5 minutes so clients reconnect and rebalance.

questions.prompt: Your site moved to HTTP/2 but still serves images from `img1.example.com`, `img2.example.com` and `img3.example.com`, a domain-sharding scheme from the HTTP/1.1 days. Each shard has its own IP and certificate. What's the effect now?

options.text: A big speed-up: three multiplexed connections are three times faster than one
options.explanation: Multiplexing on one connection already removes the reason for sharding. Extra connections add setup cost and compete with each other; they don't triple speed.

options.text: Each shard costs its own DNS lookup, TCP and TLS handshakes and slow start, and splits traffic across separate congestion windows and priority schemes; removing the shards usually helps
options.explanation: Correct. Sharding existed to get around the 6-connection limit. Under HTTP/2 it brings back the handshake cost and defeats the single-connection design.

options.text: No effect, because browsers merge all subdomains into one HTTP/2 connection automatically
options.explanation: Browsers can only *coalesce* connections when the hostnames resolve to the same IP and one certificate covers them all. Separate IPs and certificates rule that out here.

options.text: Images will fail to load, because HTTP/2 forbids multiple hostnames
options.explanation: HTTP/2 has no such rule. Pages load resources from many origins all the time.

questions.workedExample:
1. HTTP/1.1 problem: one request at a time per connection, ~6 connections per origin → shard to get more connections.
2. HTTP/2: multiple concurrent streams, subject to negotiated limits on one connection → that problem is gone.
3. Keeping shards: each of the 3 extra origins needs its own DNS lookup, TCP handshake and TLS handshake (about 3 extra round trips each) and starts its own fresh slow-start window.
4. Each connection is also prioritised separately, so the browser can't order images against CSS and scripts globally.
5. Fix: serve from one origin, or make the shards coalescible (same IP, one certificate covering all names).

lessons.title: QUIC streams, discovery and migration
lessons.summary: Explain HTTP/3’s loss isolation and the deployment conditions for discovery, fallback and migration.
lessons.body:
HTTP/3 runs HTTP over QUIC rather than one ordered TCP byte stream. The diagrams below isolate application-stream delivery from the connection-wide effects of congestion control.

## HTTP/3 and QUIC: fixing transport HOL blocking

HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) runs over **QUIC** (RFC 9000, 2021), a transport built on UDP. QUIC re-implements reliability and congestion control, and it tracks **ordering per stream**:

- A loss of application stream data does not create TCP-style ordering dependencies between otherwise independent streams.
- Other streams keep flowing.

```
QUIC packets: [A1][B1][xx][A2][C2]
                  lost ^ (B2)
A1, A2, C2 delivered at once.
Only stream B waits for B2.
```

Two subtleties. Ordering still holds *within* a stream, so a loss does stall that one stream. And congestion control is still per connection, so loss slows the whole connection's sending rate even though it no longer blocks delivery. HTTP/3 also replaced HPACK with **QPACK**, because HPACK assumes headers arrive in order, which would have reintroduced cross-stream blocking. QPACK bounds and manages header dependencies; it does not eliminate every possible cross-stream dependency.

QUIC brings several other wins:

1. **Combined handshake.** Transport and TLS 1.3 are negotiated together in the same packets: 1 RTT for a new connection instead of TCP's 1 plus TLS's 1, and **0-RTT** for resumption, where the request rides in the very first flight (with replay caveats; see the TLS lesson).
2. **Connection migration.** Nonzero *connection IDs* let endpoints identify connections across changes to the IP/port 4-tuple. A phone can keep its connection when changing networks if migration is supported and permitted; path validation and connection-ID handling still matter.
3. **Encrypted application traffic.** QUIC encrypts application data and protects parts of its transport headers, reducing middlebox dependence on protocol details. Some routing fields stay visible. The first setup packets use publicly derivable keys, so their TLS ClientHello is observable unless ECH protects it.
4. **User-space implementation.** It can evolve with app releases, not OS kernel upgrades.

Costs and caveats:

- **CPU:** UDP processing in user space has historically cost more CPU than kernel TCP (improving with offloads like GSO).
- **Blocked UDP:** some corporate networks block UDP 443. Browsers fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP.
- **Discovery:** browsers usually learn about HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc` header on an HTTP/2 response, or from a DNS `HTTPS` record, so the first visit is often HTTP/2.
- **Load balancing:** migration needs packets to keep reaching the endpoint with connection state. A balancer that hashes only the changing 4-tuple can send them to another backend; connection-ID-aware routing or equivalent forwarding support avoids that failure.

## Side by side

| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | TCP | QUIC/UDP |
| Concurrency | ~6 conns | Streams, 1 conn | Streams, 1 conn |
| HTTP HOL | Yes | No | No |
| TCP HOL | Per conn | Yes, all streams | No |
| New conn setup | 2 RTT | 2 RTT | 1 RTT |
| Resumed, 0-RTT | 1 RTT | 1 RTT | 0 RTT |

Setup figures assume TLS 1.3 and count round trips before the request can be sent. A full TLS 1.2 handshake adds one more RTT over TCP. With TLS 1.3 0-RTT over TCP, the TCP handshake still has to happen first, which is why it's 1 RTT rather than 0.

## Key takeaways

- QUIC tracks application ordering per stream, but congestion control is still shared across the connection.
- A combined transport/TLS handshake saves a setup round trip; early data carries replay caveats.
- Migration needs connection-ID-aware routing, discovery may delay first-visit HTTP/3, and blocked UDP needs TCP fallback.

## Further reading

- [QUIC (RFC 9000)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [HTTP/3 (RFC 9114)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)
- [Service binding and HTTPS records (RFC 9460)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460)

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine advantages of HTTP/3 (QUIC) over HTTP/2 (TCP + TLS)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loss of application-stream data need not block delivery on unrelated streams
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC tracks ordering per stream, so loss on stream A doesn't hold back streams B and C.

options.text: Connections can survive a client's IP address changing, for example Wi-Fi to 4G
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC identifies connections by connection ID rather than the IP/port 4-tuple, so it can migrate when the network changes.

options.text: Transport and TLS handshakes are combined, so a new connection needs 1 RTT instead of 2
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake, and resumption can use 0-RTT.

options.text: It needs less CPU than TCP on servers
options.explanation: Generally the opposite: QUIC runs in user space with per-packet encryption, and has historically cost more CPU than kernel TCP, though offloads are narrowing the gap.

options.text: It works on every network, because UDP is never blocked
options.explanation: Some enterprise firewalls block or throttle UDP 443. That's why browsers keep an HTTP/2 fallback.

questions.workedExample:
Check each claim against how QUIC works:

1. **Per-stream ordering** → no transport HOL across streams. (yes)
2. **Connection IDs** → migration across networks. (yes)
3. **Integrated TLS 1.3** → 1 RTT new, 0-RTT resume. (yes)
4. CPU: user-space UDP plus encryption per packet → typically *more* CPU. (no)
5. UDP blocking exists → fallback is needed. (no)

questions.prompt: You enable HTTP/3 on your CDN. Real-user monitoring shows that on a user's *first* visit, almost all requests still use HTTP/2, yet repeat visits use HTTP/3. Why?

options.text: HTTP/3 only works after a TLS session ticket has been cached
options.explanation: Session tickets enable 0-RTT resumption, but a full 1-RTT HTTP/3 handshake works without them. Tickets aren't required for HTTP/3 at all.

options.text: Browsers learn that an origin supports HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc` header (or DNS `HTTPS` record) and so typically start with TCP on the first contact
options.explanation: Correct. Without prior knowledge, the browser connects over TCP; the response's `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` advertises HTTP/3, which is then used for later connections. Publishing an `HTTPS` DNS record can enable HTTP/3 from the start.

options.text: QUIC needs the server to pre-warm a congestion window per client
options.explanation: QUIC uses normal congestion control starting from an initial window, like TCP. There's no per-client pre-warming requirement.

options.text: The CDN deliberately disables HTTP/3 on first visits for security
options.explanation: There's no such security policy. The behaviour comes from how clients discover HTTP/3 support.

questions.workedExample:
1. A URL says `https://`, not which HTTP version to use. TCP+TLS with ALPN is the safe default.
2. The server replies (over HTTP/2) with `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400`.
3. The browser caches that hint for `ma` seconds and tries QUIC next time, racing it against TCP in case UDP is blocked.
4. To get HTTP/3 on the very first connection, publish a DNS `HTTPS` record (RFC 9460) with `alpn=h3`, which the browser can fetch alongside the `A` record.

link.title: RFC 9460: SVCB and HTTPS resource records

questions.prompt: A QUIC connection has independent streams A, B and C. One packet carrying only B application data is lost; later A/C bytes arrive in order with no missing header/control dependencies. Assume the loss triggers congestion-window reduction. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The A and C data that arrived can be delivered to the application straight away
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC orders data per stream, so a gap in stream B doesn't hold back other streams.

options.text: Stream B's data after the gap waits until the lost data is retransmitted
options.explanation: Correct. Ordering still applies *within* a stream, so B stalls until the gap is filled.

options.text: The connection's congestion controller treats the loss as a congestion signal, slowing sending for all streams
options.explanation: Correct. Congestion control is per connection in QUIC, so loss still reduces the rate for everything, even though it no longer blocks delivery.

options.text: All three streams stall, just as they would over TCP
options.explanation: That's HTTP/2's problem. Avoiding cross-stream blocking is the main reason QUIC exists.

options.text: The lost data is never resent, because QUIC runs over UDP
options.explanation: QUIC implements its own acknowledgements and retransmission on top of UDP; it's a reliable transport.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the three things loss can affect:

1. **Delivery of other streams:** QUIC keeps a reorder buffer per stream → A and C unaffected.
2. **Delivery of the same stream:** in-order within B → B waits for the retransmission.
3. **Sending rate:** one congestion window per connection → everyone slows a bit.

So HTTP/3 removes *cross-stream* head-of-line blocking, not every effect of loss. And reliability is still there: QUIC detects the loss from its ACKs and resends the missing frames in a new packet.

questions.prompt: You enable HTTP/3 behind an L4 load balancer that hashes each UDP packet's 4-tuple (source and destination IP and port) to pick a backend. Users on phones report that downloads restart whenever they walk out of Wi-Fi range onto mobile data. Why?

options.text: QUIC doesn't support connection migration
options.explanation: It does: connections are identified by a connection ID, so they can survive an address change. The migration is failing at the load balancer, not in the protocol.

options.text: Mobile networks block HTTP/3
options.explanation: If mobile networks blocked UDP, the connection would fall back to HTTP/2, not restart mid-download after a network change.

options.text: The phone's new IP address changes the 4-tuple, so the balancer hashes its packets to a different backend that has no state or keys for the connection
options.explanation: Correct. The client migrated correctly, but the balancer routed by 4-tuple. Route by QUIC connection ID (for example with a QUIC-aware balancer that decodes server-chosen IDs) so packets keep reaching the same backend.

options.text: TLS session tickets expire when the IP changes
options.explanation: Tickets aren't tied to the client's IP. And migration doesn't need a new handshake at all; the existing connection continues.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before: phone on Wi-Fi, 4-tuple `(198.51.100.4:51000 → VIP:443)` → hashes to backend 3.
2. Phone switches to mobile data: new source IP and port → new 4-tuple.
3. QUIC on the phone continues the same connection using a valid server-issued connection ID (normally a different ID on a new path for privacy).
4. The L4 balancer hashes the *new* 4-tuple → backend 7, which has never seen this connection → it can't decrypt and drops or resets.
5. Fix: have backends encode a routing hint in the connection IDs they issue and have the balancer route on it (the IETF QUIC-LB work describes this), or use a QUIC-aware balancer.

questions.prompt: A site advertises HTTP/3 and also serves HTTPS over TCP. A browser supports TCP fallback; the customer's network blocks outbound UDP but permits TCP 443. What happens?

options.text: The site is unreachable from that network until HTTP/3 is disabled
options.explanation: Here the server and browser both support the permitted TCP path, so blocking UDP does not make the site unreachable. This is not a guarantee for every possible client or deployment.

options.text: The site works over HTTP/2 (or HTTP/1.1) on TCP, perhaps after a short delay the first time QUIC is tried and fails
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers race or fall back from QUIC to TCP, and remember that QUIC failed for a while. Users lose HTTP/3's benefits but nothing breaks.

options.text: The browser tunnels QUIC over TCP port 443
options.explanation: Browsers don't encapsulate QUIC in TCP; they just use HTTP/2 over TCP and TLS instead.

options.text: Requests succeed over UDP port 53 instead
options.explanation: Browsers don't move web traffic to the DNS port. UDP 53 is for DNS queries to resolvers.

questions.workedExample:
1. Discovery via `Alt-Svc` or an `HTTPS` DNS record tells the browser HTTP/3 is *available*, not mandatory.
2. The browser attempts QUIC on UDP 443; the packets are dropped.
3. It has a TCP connection racing alongside (or starts one after a short timeout) and uses HTTP/2 over it.
4. It marks QUIC as broken for that network for a while, so later loads go straight to TCP.

For browser access across networks that block UDP, retain a healthy HTTPS-over-TCP fallback, using HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 as supported.

lessons.title: TLS 1.3 key exchange and identity
lessons.summary: Follow the encrypted handshake and distinguish certificate authentication from ephemeral key agreement.
lessons.body:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is what puts the S in HTTPS. It gives a connection three properties:

- **Confidentiality:** nobody on the path can read the traffic.
- **Integrity:** nobody can modify it undetected.
- **Authentication:** the client knows it's talking to the real `bank.example.com`, not an impostor.

For system design, TLS matters because of its **latency cost** (extra round trips), its **CPU cost** (key exchange) and the architectural question of **where you terminate it**.

## The TLS 1.3 handshake

A normal certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 8446, 2018), without retry or early data, needs one round trip before the client sends application data:

```
Client                       Server
  |-- ClientHello ------------>|
  |   versions, ciphers,       |
  |   key share, SNI, ALPN     |
  |                            |
  |<-- ServerHello ------------|
  |    key share               |
  |    {EncryptedExtensions}   |
  |    {Certificate}           |
  |    {CertificateVerify}     |
  |    {Finished}              |
  |                            |
  |-- {Finished} + {GET /} --->|
  |<-- {200 OK} ---------------|
```

Step by step:

1. **ClientHello.** The client lists supported versions and cipher suites, and *guesses* a key-exchange group, sending its public key share up front. It includes **SNI** (the hostname) and **ALPN** (which protocols it speaks, e.g. `h2`, `http/1.1`).
2. **ServerHello.** The server picks parameters, sends its own key share, and both sides now derive the same secret via (EC)DHE key exchange. Everything after this is encrypted, including the certificate.
3. **Certificate + CertificateVerify.** The server proves it owns the private key matching its certificate by signing the handshake transcript.
4. **Finished.** Both sides confirm the handshake wasn't tampered with. The client can send its HTTP request immediately alongside its Finished message.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Mixing paint in public
> Two people openly agree on a common base colour. Each secretly picks a colour of their own, mixes it into the base and hands the mixture over in public. Each then adds their own secret colour to the mixture they received, and both end up with the same final colour. An onlooker saw the base and both mixtures but cannot practically un-mix them to find either secret.
>
> **How it maps:** the base colour is the agreed key-exchange group, each secret colour is an ephemeral private key and each public mixture is a key share sent in the ClientHello or ServerHello. The final colour is the secret both endpoints derive, from which the session keys come. Because the secret colours are fresh for every connection, stealing the certificate key later does not reveal them: that is forward secrecy.
>
> **Where it stops:** mixing paint does not tell you who you are mixing with; an attacker in the middle could mix separately with each side. That is why the server also signs the handshake with its certificate key (CertificateVerify). The real protection rests on mathematical problems that are hard to reverse, not on colours being hard to separate.

**A full TLS 1.2 handshake takes two round trips.** In the first, the client offers options and the server replies with its choice, certificate and key-exchange parameters. Only in the second does the client send its key share and both sides exchange Finished. (Extensions like TLS False Start let a TLS 1.2 client send data a round trip early, and a resumed TLS 1.2 session takes one round trip, but a full handshake is two.)

If the server doesn't support the group the TLS 1.3 client guessed, it replies with a **HelloRetryRequest** and the client tries again, costing an extra round trip. Clients offer supported groups such as X25519; the exact preference and use of hybrid post-quantum groups depend on implementation and version.

TLS 1.3 also dropped legacy, insecure options (RSA key exchange, CBC ciphers, SHA-1), and certificate-based handshakes use ephemeral key agreement for **forward secrecy**: later theft of the certificate private key does not decrypt recorded sessions. PSK-only resumption is an exception, and 0-RTT early data lacks forward secrecy against later compromise of its PSK.

## Key takeaways

- ClientHello carries a key share; the server’s response lets both endpoints derive secrets in one round trip.
- CertificateVerify proves possession of the certificate private key; (EC)DHE supplies ephemeral agreement.
- HelloRetryRequest adds a trip, and early data or PSK-only resumption has different forward-secrecy guarantees.

## Further reading

- [TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446)
- [TLS (High Performance Browser Networking)](https://hpbn.co/transport-layer-security-tls/)

questions.prompt: Why does a TLS 1.3 full handshake need only one round trip, when TLS 1.2 needed two?

options.text: The client sends its key share in the very first message, guessing the key-exchange group, so both sides can derive keys after one exchange
options.explanation: Correct. In TLS 1.2, the client only sends its key share in the second round trip, after seeing the server's choice. TLS 1.3 collapses this by having the client send a key share up front.

options.text: TLS 1.3 skips certificate verification
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 still sends and verifies the server certificate on every full handshake; it just encrypts it. Authentication wasn't removed.

options.text: TLS 1.3 runs over UDP
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 normally runs over TCP. QUIC uses TLS 1.3 over UDP, but the 1-RTT handshake is a property of TLS 1.3 itself.

options.text: TLS 1.3 uses smaller certificates
options.explanation: Certificate size does not change the protocol’s logical handshake sequence. An oversized certificate flight can nevertheless add transport delay when it exceeds the initial congestion window; TLS 1.3’s main saving here comes from restructuring key exchange.

questions.workedExample:
1. TLS 1.2: RTT 1 = client offers options, server picks a cipher and sends its certificate and key parameters; RTT 2 = client sends its key share, then both exchange Finished.
2. TLS 1.3: the ClientHello already contains an (EC)DHE public key for a likely group (e.g. X25519).
3. The server replies with its own share and can immediately encrypt the certificate and Finished.
4. Client verifies and sends Finished **plus its HTTP request**.
5. Saving at 100 ms RTT: 100 ms per new connection. (If the guess is wrong, a HelloRetryRequest costs an extra RTT.)

questions.prompt: Which statements about a certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 full handshake using (EC)DHE, without ECH, are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The server's certificate travels encrypted
options.explanation: Correct. Keys are derived right after ServerHello, so the certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished are all encrypted, unlike in TLS 1.2.

options.text: The SNI hostname is encrypted by default
options.explanation: SNI sits in the ClientHello, before any keys exist, so it's in the clear unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

options.text: This handshake uses ephemeral (EC)DHE, so later theft of the certificate private key does not decrypt recorded sessions
options.explanation: Correct. TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange; the long-term key only signs the handshake, giving forward secrecy.

options.text: Static RSA key exchange is still allowed for compatibility
options.explanation: It was removed precisely because it gives no forward secrecy. RSA keys can still be used for *signatures*, just not for key transport.

options.text: If the server doesn't support the key-exchange group the client guessed, a HelloRetryRequest costs an extra round trip
options.explanation: Correct. The client then resends its ClientHello with a share for a group the server accepts.

questions.workedExample:
Go message by message:

1. **ClientHello** (clear): versions, ciphers, key share, SNI, ALPN.
2. **ServerHello** (clear): chosen parameters and the server's key share. Both sides now derive handshake keys.
3. **Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished**: encrypted.
4. Key shares are fresh for each connection → **forward secrecy**.
5. Wrong group guess → HelloRetryRequest → +1 RTT; clients guess common groups (X25519, or a hybrid post-quantum group) to avoid it.

lessons.title: Certificate chains and renewal
lessons.summary: Validate names and chains, automate shorter certificate lifetimes and avoid oversized handshake flights.
lessons.body:
A certificate is the server’s name-to-key evidence. Correct hostname coverage, a complete chain and timely renewal matter separately from the key-exchange protocol.

## Certificates and the chain of trust

A certificate binds a public key to one or more names, signed by a **certificate authority (CA)**.

```
Root CA  (in OS/browser trust store)
   |
   | signs
   v
Intermediate CA
   |
   | signs
   v
Leaf: shop.example.com
```

The client verifies:

1. The leaf certificate's names (in the **Subject Alternative Name** field) include the hostname. A wildcard `*.example.com` covers `shop.example.com` but not `a.b.example.com` or `example.com`.
2. Each certificate in the chain is signed by the next, ending at a **root** in its trust store.
3. The applicable validity periods and certificate constraints pass validation. Revocation handling depends on client policy; a successful connection does not prove that every certificate was checked online.

The server must send the leaf **and intermediates**. A missing intermediate is a classic bug: it works in desktop browsers (which may cache or fetch intermediates) but fails in mobile apps and `curl`.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A letter of introduction from someone you trust
> A stranger shows you a letter saying "this is Sam", signed by a manager you've never heard of. Attached is a second letter, signed by a company director whose signature you already know, vouching for that manager. You trust Sam only because you can follow the signatures back to someone you already trusted.
>
> **How it maps:** Sam's letter is the leaf certificate binding a name to a key, the manager is the intermediate CA and the director you already know is a root in your trust store. Forgetting to attach the second letter is the classic missing-intermediate bug.
>
> **Where it stops:** a TLS client checks cryptographic signatures, names, validity dates and constraints mechanically rather than recognising handwriting. Holding a certificate proves nothing by itself: the server must also prove it has the matching private key during the handshake.

### Issuance and automation

**Let's Encrypt** offers free certificates and automated issuance through ACME. As checked on 29 October 2026, its default classic profile is scheduled to move from 90 to 64 days on 10 February 2027, then to 45 days on 16 February 2028; its optional tlsserver profile moved to 45 days in May 2026. Schedules like these can change, so check the CA’s current announcements. The CA/Browser Forum maximum for newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates became 200 days on 15 March 2026 and is scheduled to become 100 days on 15 March 2027 and 47 days on 15 March 2029. Automate renewal and monitor expiry to make these shorter cycles manageable. These public-trust requirements do not automatically govern a private PKI.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> No comparative outage dataset or reproducible TLS performance benchmark accompanies this lesson. Claims that certificate expiry is a leading outage cause, and universal throughput or signature-speed estimates, are omitted; measure your deployment.

### Revocation and transparency

- **Revocation** (CRLs, OCSP) is unreliable in practice; many clients don't check it strictly, and browsers instead push compressed revocation lists to themselves (Chrome's CRLSets, Firefox's CRLite). **OCSP stapling** lets the server attach a fresh signed status to the handshake, saving the client a lookup, but OCSP is in decline: the CA/Browser Forum made it optional, and Let's Encrypt shut its OCSP service down in 2025 in favour of CRLs. Shorter lifetimes complement revocation by limiting how long an unrevoked certificate can remain valid.
- **Certificate Transparency (CT)** uses public append-only logs; browser CT policies require qualifying publicly trusted certificates to have evidence of logging. Private certificates are not universally subject to CT. You can monitor them for certificates issued for your domains that you didn't request.
- **CAA DNS records** restrict which CAs may issue for your domain.

### Chain size also affects latency

Keep certificate chains small. For comparable certificate fields, ECDSA P-256 uses smaller keys and signatures than RSA-2048; actual certificate size and signing time depend on the chain and implementation. As the earlier TCP lesson showed, a first flight larger than the initial congestion window must wait for acknowledgements before the rest can be sent. Send necessary intermediates, omit an unnecessary root, and consider negotiated certificate compression. This is a size-dependent transport cost, not an extra round trip inherent in RSA key exchange.

## Key takeaways

- Validate the leaf hostname and a chain to a trusted root; send the required intermediates.
- A wildcard covers one label, and successful validation does not prove universal online revocation checking.
- Automate public-certificate renewal and keep the served chain lean enough for the intended transport.

## Further reading

- [How Let’s Encrypt works](https://letsencrypt.org/how-it-works/)
- [Public certificate lifetime schedule (CA/Browser Forum)](https://cabforum.org/2025/04/11/ballot-sc081v3-introduce-schedule-of-reducing-validity-and-data-reuse-periods/)
- [Certificate lifetime changes (Let’s Encrypt)](https://letsencrypt.org/2025/12/02/from-90-to-45)
- [TLS certificate compression (RFC 8879)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8879)

questions.prompt: A wildcard certificate is issued for `*.example.com`. Which hostname will it **not** be valid for?

options.text: `shop.example.com`
options.explanation: A wildcard matches exactly one label in the leftmost position, and `shop` is one label, so this is covered.

options.text: `api.example.com`
options.explanation: `api` is a single leftmost label, so `*.example.com` covers it.

options.text: `eu.api.example.com`
options.explanation: Correct. The wildcard matches only one label. `eu.api` is two labels, so you'd need `*.api.example.com` or an explicit name.

options.text: `www.example.com`
options.explanation: `www` is a single label, so it matches the wildcard.

questions.workedExample:
1. `*` replaces exactly **one** DNS label (the text between dots), in the leftmost position.
2. `shop.example.com`, `api.example.com`, `www.example.com` → one label before `example.com` → valid.
3. `eu.api.example.com` → two labels → **invalid**.
4. Also note `*.example.com` doesn't cover the bare `example.com`; add it as a separate SAN.

questions.prompt: After a certificate renewal, your site works in Chrome on desktop, but your Android app and `curl` fail with 'unable to verify the first certificate'. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The new certificate uses TLS 1.3
options.explanation: Certificates are not tied to a single TLS version. The reported error concerns chain validation; TLS-version support depends on the particular client and library.

options.text: The root CA was removed from all trust stores
options.explanation: If the root were untrusted, desktop Chrome would fail too. The fact that only some clients fail points to a missing intermediate.

options.text: DNS is returning the wrong IP for the app
options.explanation: A wrong IP would usually give a name mismatch or connection error. 'Unable to verify the first certificate' specifically means the client couldn't find the issuer of the leaf.

options.text: The server is sending only the leaf certificate, not the intermediate; desktop browsers fill the gap themselves but other clients don't
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers can cache intermediates or fetch them via the certificate's AIA URL. Many other clients don't, so the chain to a trusted root is broken.

questions.workedExample:
1. The client needs a path: leaf → intermediate → root (in its trust store).
2. The server must send **leaf + intermediate(s)**; the root is already on the client.
3. After renewal, the config often points at `cert.pem` (leaf only) instead of `fullchain.pem`.
4. Chrome on desktop hides this by fetching the intermediate itself; `curl` and many mobile stacks don't.
5. Check with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts` and fix the chain file.

questions.prompt: A team previously bought one-year publicly trusted TLS certificates and renewed them by hand each January. What do the CA/Browser Forum's lifetime changes mean for that process?

options.text: Nothing, because one-year certificates remain valid for public websites
options.explanation: Public TLS certificate lifetimes are being cut in stages, starting at 200 days in March 2026, so one-year certificates can no longer be issued for public sites.

options.text: They can avoid the change by buying certificates in bulk in advance
options.explanation: Certificates issued now still carry the shorter maximum lifetime, so stockpiling doesn't help.

options.text: Maximum lifetimes drop to 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from 2027 and 47 days from 2029, so they need automated renewal (for example ACME) rather than a yearly manual task
options.explanation: Correct. Maximum validity periods shorten in stages, so an annual renewal task no longer suffices. Automation and expiry monitoring reduce the operational risk of more frequent replacement.

options.text: Shorter lifetimes only apply to Let's Encrypt certificates
options.explanation: The CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements apply to every publicly trusted CA, paid or free.

questions.workedExample:
1. The public-TLS maximum became 200 days on 15 March 2026 and is scheduled to fall to 100 days on 15 March 2027 and 47 days on 15 March 2029.
2. A 47-day certificate renewed with some safety margin (for example at about two-thirds of its life) needs replacing roughly every month: far too often to rely on someone remembering.
3. Frequent manual renewal increases the chance of an operational mistake; an outage is not inevitable, but the risk grows with every hand-run step.
4. Use ACME or a managed certificate service, test renewal, and monitor expiry. A private PKI follows its own policy, not these public-trust limits.

questions.prompt: Assume TCP's initial congestion window is ten 1,460-byte segments and the server has no earlier opportunity to grow it. After a switch to an RSA-4096 leaf and two intermediates (about 18 KB of certificates), distant clients need an extra handshake round trip. Why?

options.text: RSA-4096 is not supported by TLS 1.3
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 accepts RSA certificates for signatures. Support isn't the issue; size is.

options.text: Clients must download intermediates separately
options.explanation: The server is sending the intermediates, which is why the flight is so large. The problem is the size of that flight.

options.text: The server's first flight is larger than TCP's initial congestion window (about 14 KB), so the server must wait for the client's ACK before sending the rest
options.explanation: Correct. The certificates overflow the initial window, so the handshake spills into a second round trip. A smaller ECDSA certificate and a trimmed chain fit in one flight.

options.text: Longer keys always add a round trip to key exchange
options.explanation: Key exchange uses ephemeral (EC)DHE shares regardless of the certificate's key size; a bigger certificate key doesn't add round trips by itself.

questions.workedExample:
1. On a new connection, TCP lets the server send only its initial congestion window before it must wait for an acknowledgement. Ten 1,460-byte segments is about 14 KB.
2. The server's first TLS flight (ServerHello, extensions, about 18 KB of certificates, CertificateVerify and Finished) is now roughly 19 KB, larger than that window.
3. So the server sends the first 14 KB, waits one round trip for the client's acknowledgement, then sends the rest: an extra round trip that distant clients notice most.

Fixes:
  - ECDSA P-256 certificates (far smaller than RSA-4096).
  - Don't send the root or unneeded cross-signs.
  - Certificate compression (RFC 8879), when both endpoints negotiate support.

lessons.title: TLS termination and service identity
lessons.summary: Choose edge termination, re-encryption or passthrough and understand mutual TLS lifecycle work.
lessons.body:
The location that decrypts traffic determines what a load balancer can route on and who holds the private key. For internal connections, encryption and service authentication are separate requirements.

## Where to terminate TLS

"Termination" is where the encrypted connection ends and traffic is decrypted. You have three main patterns:

| Pattern | Where decrypted | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Edge termination | LB / CDN | Simple; internal hop plaintext |
| Re-encryption | LB, then again at app | Encrypts both hops; adds another TLS connection and requires backend authentication policy |
| Passthrough | App server only | LB can't see HTTP (L4 only) |

```
Edge termination:
Client ==TLS==> LB --HTTP--> App

Re-encryption:
Client ==TLS==> LB ==TLS==> App

Passthrough:
Client ==========TLS========> App
           (LB forwards TCP)
```

**Edge termination** is the common default. The load balancer holds the certificate, offloads crypto from app servers, and can inspect HTTP to route by path, add headers like `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and apply a WAF.

But "plaintext inside the network" is increasingly unacceptable. **Zero-trust** designs and the risk of attackers moving laterally inside networks motivate **re-encryption** or **mutual TLS (mTLS)** between services. Validate backend identities as well as encrypting connections; encryption alone does not establish which service you reached. Service meshes automate mTLS so every service gets a certificate and identity.

**Passthrough** is used when the app must hold the key (end-to-end requirements) or needs the raw TLS session (e.g. for client certificates). The load balancer can still route by **SNI**, which is visible in the ClientHello, but can't see paths or headers. **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** hides the real SNI inside an encrypted inner ClientHello; an SNI-routing balancer then sees only the outer, public name unless it holds the ECH keys itself.

> [!note] Keys at the edge
> Edge termination on a CDN means a third party holds your private key or terminates on your behalf. For highly sensitive keys, options include short-lived delegated credentials or "keyless" setups where the CDN calls back to your own key server for the signing step.

## mTLS: when the client authenticates too

In normal TLS only the server presents a certificate. In **mutual TLS**, the client does too. That's common for:

- Service-to-service traffic in a mesh (Istio, Linkerd issue a certificate per workload).
- B2B APIs and payment networks.
- IoT devices with a certificate burned in at manufacture.

The hard part isn't the protocol but **certificate lifecycle**: issuing, rotating (at a configured lifetime and renewal interval) and revoking at scale. That's what mesh control planes and tools like SPIFFE/SPIRE automate.

## Key takeaways

- Edge termination enables HTTP routing; re-encryption protects a separate backend connection.
- Authenticate backend identities as well as encrypting their traffic.
- Passthrough can use visible SNI but cannot see HTTP paths; mTLS requires client certificates and lifecycle management.

## Further reading

- [TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446)
- [Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9849)
- [What is Istio?](https://istio.io/latest/docs/concepts/what-is-istio/)

questions.prompt: You want your load balancer to route `/api/*` to one service and `/static/*` to another, while traffic between the load balancer and services must also be encrypted. Which TLS pattern fits?

options.text: TLS passthrough to the services
options.explanation: With passthrough the load balancer never decrypts, so it can't see the URL path and can't route on `/api` vs `/static`. It could only route by SNI.

options.text: Terminate at the load balancer and re-encrypt to the services (or use mTLS)
options.explanation: Correct. Decrypting at the load balancer lets it read paths and headers for L7 routing; opening a new TLS connection to each backend keeps the internal hop encrypted.

options.text: Terminate at the load balancer, then plain HTTP to the services
options.explanation: This allows path routing but leaves the internal hop unencrypted, which breaks the requirement.

options.text: Use a single TLS session from the client through to every service
options.explanation: A TLS session is between two endpoints. One session can't fan out to multiple services and still let the middle box read the path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Requirement A: route by path → the LB must **see HTTP** → it must decrypt.
2. Requirement B: internal hop encrypted → the LB must **open a new TLS connection** to backends.
3. Passthrough fails A; edge-only termination fails B.
4. Re-encryption satisfies both. The cost is two TLS sessions per request path, mitigated by keeping the LB→backend connections pooled.
