questions.prompt: A TLS-passthrough L4 load balancer fronts 200 customer domains, each with its own certificate on different backend clusters. How can it send each connection to the right cluster without decrypting?

options.text: It reads the SNI hostname from the unencrypted ClientHello
options.explanation: Correct. SNI is sent in clear in the ClientHello (unless Encrypted Client Hello is used), so an L4/TLS-aware proxy can route on it without holding any keys.

options.text: It reads the `Host` header
options.explanation: The `Host` header is inside the encrypted HTTP request, so a passthrough balancer can't see it.

options.text: It uses a different destination port for each domain
options.explanation: Clients all connect to port 443 for HTTPS, so ports can't distinguish 200 domains.

options.text: It can't; passthrough requires one IP address per domain
options.explanation: That was true before SNI was widely supported. Today SNI-based routing makes shared IPs work with passthrough.

questions.workedExample:
1. Passthrough means the LB sees only TCP plus the cleartext parts of TLS.
2. The ClientHello includes `server_name` (SNI), e.g. `shop.customer42.com`.
3. The LB peeks at it (HAProxy `req.ssl_sni`, Envoy's TLS inspector) and picks the backend cluster.
4. Caveat: **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** hides the real SNI behind an outer, public name, which would break this unless the LB itself holds the ECH keys.

lessons.title: Resumption, setup cost and replay
lessons.summary: Choose ways to cut TLS setup, make tickets work across a fleet and decide which requests tolerate early data.
lessons.body:
Once certificate trust and termination are understood, the remaining question is how to pay for fewer or shorter handshakes. The figures below exclude DNS and assume no handshake retry, loss or extra processing.

## The latency cost, and how to reduce it

A new HTTPS connection over TCP waits for **one TCP round trip and one TLS 1.3 round trip** before the request can go out. The time spent on setup is simply that number of round trips multiplied by the round-trip time, so there are two ways to cut it: do fewer round trips, or make each one shorter. At an illustrative 100 ms RTT that is 200 ms of pure setup; at a CDN edge 10 ms away the same two trips cost about 20 ms.

Ways to cut it:

1. **Use TLS 1.3.** Saves a full RTT over TLS 1.2.
2. **Session resumption.** The server hands the client a *session ticket*; next time, the handshake skips certificate exchange and verification (less CPU and fewer bytes).
3. **0-RTT (early data).** With a ticket, TLS 1.3 lets the client send its request *in the first flight*. Setup cost on resumption drops to just the TCP handshake (or nothing extra with QUIC).
4. **Terminate close to the user.** Handshakes at a CDN edge 10 ms away cost 20 ms, not 200 ms. The edge keeps warm, long-lived connections to the origin.
5. **Reuse connections.** The best handshake is the one you don't do.
6. **Keep certificate chains small.** For comparable certificate fields, ECDSA P-256 uses smaller keys and signatures than RSA-2048; actual certificate size and signing time depend on the chain and implementation. Oversized chains can overflow TCP's initial window and add an RTT.

Putting the round trips together, before the first request byte can leave the client:

| Setup | New | Resumed |
|---|---|---|
| TCP + TLS 1.2 | 3 RTT | 2 RTT |
| TCP + TLS 1.3 | 2 RTT | 2 (1 with 0-RTT) |
| QUIC | 1 RTT | 1 (0 with 0-RTT) |

Note that plain TLS 1.3 resumption *without* early data saves CPU and bytes, not round trips: it still takes a full round trip before the request goes out.

> [!warning] 0-RTT replay
> Early data has no protection against replay across connections: an attacker who captures the first flight can resend it. Servers must assess **replay safety**, not merely idempotency. RFC 8470 permits clients, absent other information, to send only safe HTTP methods in early data. Even a nominal `GET` requires care if its implementation has sensitive side effects. When Cloudflare launched 0-RTT in 2017, it answered only `GET` requests without query parameters in early data, and tagged them with a header so the origin could spot replays. RFC 8470 standardises this pattern: a proxy adds `Early-Data: 1`, and an origin that won't risk it replies `425 Too Early`, making the client retry after the handshake completes.

### CPU cost

TLS CPU cost includes bulk encryption, handshake signatures and key exchange. Their relative cost depends on hardware, cryptographic library, algorithms, record sizes and connection reuse. Benchmark representative traffic before sizing load balancers; resumption and connection reuse can reduce handshake work.

### Tickets across a fleet

In an encrypted stateless-ticket design, the receiving server needs a compatible ticket-encryption key to recover the resumable state. If each terminating node has a different key, a returning client routed to another node may need a full handshake. A securely distributed, rotated key set can support resumption across servers; other designs use opaque ticket identifiers and shared server-side state. NGINX documents explicit ticket keys for configurations that need the same key on several servers. Protect the keys: compromise can expose early data or PSK-only traffic, even though it does not automatically decrypt past traffic protected by fresh (EC)DHE.

## Key takeaways

- TLS 1.3 resumption without early data saves bytes and work but still requires a TLS round trip.
- Early data can save that trip only when the application can tolerate replay safely.
- Reused connections and nearby termination cut setup cost; ticket designs must work across the terminating fleet.

## Further reading

- [TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446)
- [Using early data in HTTP (RFC 8470)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8470)
- [Session ticket keys (NGINX)](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_ssl_module.html#ssl_session_ticket_key)

questions.prompt: A mobile app's users are 150 ms from your only region. Which measures reduce the latency added by TLS for them? Select all that apply.

options.text: Upgrade from TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3
options.explanation: Correct. That removes one round trip from every full handshake, saving one 150 ms trip per new connection.

options.text: Terminate TLS at CDN edges close to users
options.explanation: Correct. The handshake round trips now cost the short RTT to the edge (e.g. 10 ms) instead of 150 ms; the edge keeps warm connections to the origin.

options.text: Keep connections alive and reuse them across requests
options.explanation: Correct. A reused connection pays no handshake at all for subsequent requests.

options.text: Switch from ECDSA to RSA-4096 certificates
options.explanation: Changing the certificate algorithm does not remove a handshake round trip. RSA-4096 certificates and signatures can increase the first-flight bytes compared with ECDSA; signing cost depends on the hardware, library and implementation, so benchmark it rather than assuming a latency reduction.

options.text: Enable session resumption with 0-RTT for requests the application can safely tolerate being replayed
options.explanation: Correct. Returning clients can send `GET` requests in the first flight, removing the TLS round trip on resumption.

questions.workedExample:
Setup cost is the number of round trips multiplied by the round-trip time, so a measure helps if it removes trips or shortens them:

- Baseline, new connection with TLS 1.2: three round trips (TCP plus two for TLS) before the request.
- TLS 1.3 → two round trips: **fewer trips**.
- 0-RTT on resumption, for replay-safe requests → only the TCP round trip remains: **fewer trips**.
- Edge termination → the handshake trips go to a nearby edge, plus one origin trip over a warm connection: **shorter trips**.
- Connection reuse → no setup at all for later requests.

Changing to RSA-4096 removes no protocol round trip; it can enlarge the first flight, and its signing cost depends on the implementation.

questions.prompt: Your team proposes enabling TLS 1.3 0-RTT for all API endpoints, including `POST /payments`. What's the main risk?

options.text: 0-RTT data is sent unencrypted
options.explanation: Early data is encrypted, but it can be replayed and lacks forward secrecy against later compromise of its PSK.

options.text: 0-RTT breaks forward secrecy for all later traffic
options.explanation: With PSK plus fresh (EC)DHE, later application traffic retains forward secrecy even though early data does not. PSK-only mode has different forward-secrecy properties.

options.text: An attacker can capture and replay the early-data request, so the payment could be processed twice
options.explanation: Correct. Captured early data can be replayed across connections. Reject payment requests in early data unless the application has explicitly designed and validated replay-safe handling; an idempotency key alone is not a complete transport replay policy.

options.text: 0-RTT doubles the handshake latency
options.explanation: 0-RTT removes handshake latency on resumption; that's the whole point. Its cost is security, not speed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Early data uses keys derived from a PSK established by a previous handshake.
2. An attacker can record and replay the first flight, potentially to a different server.
3. A correctly implemented safe product read can tolerate repetition; a payment may charge twice.
4. Clients should use safe methods unless they have additional safety information. A proxy marks forwarded early requests with `Early-Data: 1`; an origin that cannot process them safely replies `425 Too Early`. Use payment idempotency controls independently.

questions.prompt: A returning client reconnects over TCP using TLS 1.3 session resumption with a valid ticket, but the server has early data (0-RTT) **disabled**. Compared with a full TLS 1.3 handshake on a new TCP connection, when can the client send its HTTP request?

options.text: Immediately, in the first packet, because resumption is 0-RTT
options.explanation: Resumption and 0-RTT are separate. Without early data, the client must still finish a one-round-trip TLS handshake before sending application data, and TCP needs its own round trip first.

options.text: One round trip earlier, because resumption skips the TLS handshake entirely
options.explanation: Resumption shortens the handshake's content (no certificate exchange), not its round-trip count. The ClientHello and ServerHello exchange still happens.

options.text: Later, because resumption adds a ticket-validation round trip
options.explanation: The server validates the ticket inside the normal handshake; there is no extra round trip.

options.text: At the same point: one TCP round trip and one TLS round trip in both cases; resumption saves CPU and bytes, not round trips
options.explanation: Correct. Resumption skips sending and verifying the certificate chain, but without early data the request still waits for the same two round trips over TCP.

questions.workedExample:
Count the round trips before the request can leave:

| Step | Full TLS 1.3 | Resumed, no early data |
|---|---|---|
| TCP SYN / SYN-ACK | 1 | 1 |
| TLS hello exchange | 1 (with certificate) | 1 (with PSK, no certificate) |

Both take two round trips. Resumption makes the second one lighter (no certificate to send or verify), which saves CPU and bytes.

Only early data changes the count: with 0-RTT the request rides with the ClientHello, after just the TCP round trip; with QUIC and 0-RTT it leaves in the very first flight. Early data needs a replay-safe request.

questions.prompt: You run 20 TLS-terminating nodes using encrypted stateless session tickets. Reconnecting clients are distributed uniformly and independently across nodes, and every node generates a different ticket-encryption key. Clients support tickets, but resumption succeeds only about 5% of the time. Why?

options.text: Clients don't support session tickets
options.explanation: Almost every modern TLS client supports resumption; a 5% rate points at the servers, not the clients.

options.text: A returning client usually lands on a different node, which can't decrypt a ticket issued with another node's key, so it falls back to a full handshake
options.explanation: Correct. With 20 independent keys, a client has roughly a 1 in 20 chance of reaching the node that issued its ticket, which matches the 5% resumption rate. Share ticket keys across the fleet (rotated frequently and distributed securely).

options.text: TLS 1.3 doesn't support resumption
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 supports resumption via pre-shared keys from session tickets; it's also what 0-RTT is built on.

options.text: Anycast encrypts tickets differently per region
options.explanation: Anycast is a routing technique and has nothing to do with ticket encryption.

questions.workedExample:
1. This implementation encrypts the resumable state into a stateless ticket using the issuing node's key; other implementations use opaque session IDs and shared server-side state.
2. A returning client presents its ticket to whichever node it reaches, chosen uniformly from 20.
3. Only the node that issued the ticket holds the right key, so resumption works only when the client happens to land there: about one time in twenty, which matches the observed 5%.
4. Every other reconnection falls back to a full handshake.

Fix: share a securely distributed, rotated ticket-key set across the fleet, or use another resumption design that works across nodes.
Note that ticket-key compromise can enable impersonation and expose early data or PSK-only traffic; it does not automatically decrypt past post-handshake traffic protected by fresh (EC)DHE.

lessons.title: L4, L7 and direct server return
lessons.summary: Choose a traffic layer for packet forwarding, request routing and response bandwidth.
lessons.body:
A load balancer sits in front of a pool of servers and decides which one handles each connection or request. It gives you three things at once:

- **Scale:** add servers behind one address.
- **Availability:** stop sending traffic to servers that fail.
- **Operability:** drain, deploy and replace servers without users noticing.

Choosing a load balancer is mostly about two questions: *at which layer does it work*, and *how does it choose a server*?

## L4 vs L7

```
        L4 (transport)
Client --TCP/UDP--> LB --> backend
  sees: IPs, ports, protocol

        L7 (application)
Client --HTTP--> LB --> backend
  sees: path, headers, cookies,
        method, gRPC service
```

| | L4 | L7 |
|---|---|---|
| Unit balanced | Connection / flow | Request |
| Sees | IP, port | URL, headers, body |
| TLS | Usually passthrough | Terminates |
| Work | Packet forwarding | HTTP parsing and proxying |
| Examples | AWS NLB, Maglev, Katran | AWS ALB, Envoy, NGINX |

**L4 load balancers** forward packets based on the 5-tuple (source IP/port, destination IP/port, protocol). They're extremely fast and protocol-agnostic: they work for databases, MQTT, SMTP, anything over TCP or UDP. Google's Maglev and Meta's Katran use software packet forwarding designed for high throughput; their achieved rates depend on hardware, packet sizes and configuration. Some use **direct server return (DSR)**: responses go straight from the backend to the client, bypassing the balancer, which matters because responses are usually much bigger than requests.

**L7 load balancers** terminate the client's connection, parse HTTP, and open (or reuse) separate connections to backends. That costs more CPU but enables:

- Routing by path or host (`/api` → API service, `/img` → image service).
- Per-request balancing of multiplexed HTTP/2 and gRPC.
- Retries, timeouts, header rewriting, auth, rate limiting, compression.
- Detailed metrics per route and status code.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A sorting office versus a mail room that opens letters
> A postal sorting office routes each envelope by the address on the outside. It never opens anything, so it is fast and handles any kind of post. A company mail room can open each letter, read it and send it to the right department, but that takes more effort per item and the authority to open the post.
>
> **How it maps:** the sorting office is an L4 balancer choosing a backend from IP addresses and ports. The mail room is an L7 balancer: it terminates TLS (opens the envelope), reads the path and headers and routes each request on its merits.
>
> **Where it stops:** an L4 balancer decides once per connection, so every later request on that connection follows the same route, whereas post is sorted item by item. An L7 balancer also does more than read and pass on: it holds a separate connection to the backend and can retry, rewrite or reject requests.

> [!tip] The common layering
> Large deployments often stack both: an L4 tier (anycast + ECMP across many machines) spreads connections over a fleet of L7 proxies, which then do the smart per-request work. The L4 tier is simple and scales; the L7 tier is flexible.

## Key takeaways

- L4 forwards transport flows; L7 understands HTTP requests and can route by path or headers.
- Direct server return lets large responses bypass an L4 balancer.
- Layering an L4 fleet ahead of L7 proxies separates connection distribution from application policy.

## Further reading

- [Application Load Balancer overview (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html)
- [Maglev (Google Research)](https://research.google/pubs/maglev-a-fast-and-reliable-software-network-load-balancer/)

questions.prompt: You need to send `/api/*` requests to one server pool and `/images/*` to another, from the same hostname. Which kind of load balancer do you need?

options.text: An L4 load balancer, because it's faster
options.explanation: L4 balancers only see IP addresses and ports. The URL path is inside the HTTP request (and usually inside TLS), so an L4 balancer can't route on it.

options.text: Round-robin DNS
options.explanation: DNS works on hostnames only; it never sees URL paths. Both paths share a hostname, so DNS can't separate them.

options.text: Either; all load balancers can route by path
options.explanation: Only balancers that understand HTTP can route by path. That's the defining difference between L4 and L7.

options.text: An L7 load balancer
options.explanation: Correct. An L7 balancer terminates the connection and parses HTTP, so it can read the path and pick a pool per request.

questions.workedExample:
1. What information is needed? The **path** (`/api` vs `/images`).
2. Where does it live? In the HTTP request line, inside the TLS-encrypted stream.
3. Who can see it? Only something that terminates TLS and parses HTTP, i.e. **L7**.
4. Examples: AWS ALB path rules, NGINX `location` blocks, Envoy route config.

questions.prompt: You serve 40 Gbps of video responses but only 1 Gbps of requests. Your software L4 balancers are saturating their network links. Which technique most directly cuts balancer bandwidth?

options.text: Switch to an L7 balancer
options.explanation: An L7 balancer proxies both directions and does more work per byte, so it would carry the full 41 Gbps and need even more capacity.

options.text: Direct server return (DSR), so backends send responses straight to clients and the balancer only handles the inbound 1 Gbps
options.explanation: Correct. With DSR, backends reply using the service IP as the source address, bypassing the balancer. It's a classic L4 technique for asymmetric traffic.

options.text: Enable sticky sessions
options.explanation: Stickiness changes which backend gets a connection, not how much data flows through the balancer.

options.text: Use weighted round robin
options.explanation: Weights change how traffic is split among backends; every byte still passes through the balancer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Without DSR, every byte in both directions passes through the balancers: the 1 Gbps of requests plus the 40 Gbps of responses.
2. DSR lets backends send responses straight to clients using the service address, so the balancers handle only the inbound requests, a small fraction of the original traffic in this simplified accounting (it ignores ACKs, encapsulation and other overhead).
3. The other options change *which* backend gets traffic, or add work per byte (L7), but every response byte would still cross the balancer.
4. Trade-offs: the return path bypasses passive response inspection, and backends and routing must be configured to accept and answer for the service address. Active health probes can still receive their own responses.

questions.prompt: For which of these requirements do you need an **L7** load balancer rather than an L4 one? Select all that apply.

options.text: Spreading individual gRPC calls from a few long-lived clients across many backends
options.explanation: Correct. gRPC multiplexes many calls over one HTTP/2 connection; only something that parses HTTP/2 can balance per call rather than per connection.

options.text: Sending requests with header `x-canary: true` to a canary pool
options.explanation: Correct. Headers are inside the (usually TLS-encrypted) HTTP request, so only an L7 balancer can read them.

options.text: Balancing PostgreSQL client connections across read replicas
options.explanation: The Postgres wire protocol isn't HTTP; an L4 balancer spreading TCP connections works fine (or a Postgres-aware proxy, which isn't an HTTP L7 balancer).

options.text: Using direct server return so responses bypass the balancer
options.explanation: DSR is an L4 technique: the balancer only forwards inbound packets. An L7 proxy must see responses, so it can't use DSR.

options.text: Routing `/checkout` and `/search` to different services on the same hostname
options.explanation: Correct. The path is part of the HTTP request, which only an L7 balancer parses.

Ask, for each requirement: **does the decision need anything above IP and port?**

| Need | Data needed | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| Per-call gRPC | HTTP/2 streams | L7 |
| Header canary | HTTP header | L7 |
| Postgres conns | TCP connection | L4 |
| DSR | IP packets | L4 |
| Path routing | URL path | L7 |

L4 decisions are made once per connection from the 5-tuple. Anything about individual requests needs L7.

lessons.title: Request cost and two-choice balancing
lessons.summary: Choose between rotation, load tracking and random sampling when request costs vary.
lessons.body:
An equal request count does not imply equal load. Start with a workload model, then decide how much live state and coordination the balancing policy needs.

## Balancing algorithms

### Round robin

Send each new request to the next server in turn. Simple, requiring only rotation state rather than load measurements, and fair **if every request costs the same and every server is identical**. Neither is usually true.

**Weighted round robin** gives bigger servers proportionally more traffic: each server's share is its weight divided by the sum of all weights. With weights 2:1:1, the big server gets half the requests and each smaller one a quarter. Weights express capacity you configured, not load you measured.

### Least connections / least outstanding requests

Send to the server with the fewest active connections (or in-flight requests). This adapts automatically: a server stuck on slow requests accumulates connections and gets fewer new ones.

It needs the balancer to track state per backend, which is easy for one balancer but approximate when there are many balancer instances, each seeing only its own traffic.

### Random, and the power of two choices

Pure random spreads load evenly *on average*, but some servers get unlucky streaks. The **power of two choices** fixes this almost for free:

1. Pick **two** servers at random.
2. Send the request to the one with fewer outstanding requests.

Work by Azar and colleagues, popularised by Michael Mitzenmacher's analysis, showed that this shrinks the worst server's load dramatically. The classic thought experiment sends as many requests as there are servers and asks how loaded the busiest server ends up.

```formula reference
L_1 ≈ ln(n) / ln(ln(n))
L_d ≈ ln(ln(n)) / ln(d)
where
L_1: the load on the busiest server, in requests, when each request goes to one server chosen at random
L_d: the same when each request samples d servers at random and joins the least loaded of them
n: the number of servers, and also the number of requests sent
d: how many servers each request samples; 2 for the power of two choices
ln: the natural logarithm, a function that grows very slowly
≈: approximately; these are the leading terms of how the load grows, with high probability, ignoring constant terms
In words: with one random choice the busiest server's load grows a little more slowly than the logarithm of the fleet size; with two choices it grows only like the logarithm of a logarithm, which barely moves even as the fleet grows a thousand-fold. A third choice improves this only by a constant factor.
```

These are asymptotic results for an idealised model, so read them as a statement about how imbalance *grows*, not as predictions for your fleet. The practical message: almost all the benefit comes from the second sample, and sampling more servers adds little.

It also avoids the **herding** problem of global least-connections, where every balancer sees the same "least loaded" server and they all pile on at once. Envoy's `LEAST_REQUEST` policy (which samples two hosts by default) and NGINX's `random two least_conn` use this idea. Select the desired policy explicitly; defaults and weighted-host behaviour depend on the Envoy configuration/API being used.

## Key takeaways

- Round robin balances counts; weights adapt server shares but do not measure current work.
- Least-outstanding-request policies adapt to slow work but have incomplete views across many balancers.
- Two random choices reduce imbalance and herding; the balls-into-bins formulas are asymptotic illustrations.

## Further reading

- [Supported load balancers (Envoy)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancers)
- [Power of two choices (HAProxy)](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/power-of-two-load-balancing)

questions.prompt: A pool has four identical servers behind round robin. Most requests take 5 ms, but 1% are report exports taking 30 s. What problem will round robin cause?

options.text: None; round robin gives each server exactly a quarter of the work
options.explanation: Round robin gives each server a quarter of the **requests**, not the work. A server that happens to receive several 30 s exports is far busier than the others but keeps getting its full share.

options.text: Servers that pick up the slow exports pile up in-flight requests and slow down, while round robin keeps sending them new traffic
options.explanation: Correct. Round robin ignores current load. A least-requests or power-of-two-choices algorithm would steer new requests away from servers busy with exports.

options.text: Round robin will crash when request times differ
options.explanation: Round robin doesn't know or care about request durations; it won't crash. It just distributes unevenly in terms of actual load.

options.text: Round robin will send all exports to the same server
options.explanation: Round robin doesn't look at request type at all. Exports land wherever the rotation happens to be.

questions.workedExample:
1. Round robin balances the **count** of requests, assuming each costs the same.
2. Here one export occupies a worker as long as thousands of normal requests (30 s versus 5 ms), so counting requests says little about load.
3. Suppose server B picks up three exports in a minute: three workers are busy for 30 s, yet B still receives a quarter of the new 5 ms requests, which queue behind them.
4. **Least outstanding requests** sees that B has more in flight and favours A, C and D.
5. Better still: move exports to a separate worker pool or asynchronous job queue so they can't starve interactive traffic.

questions.prompt: You run 50 independent L7 proxy instances, each doing global *least-connections* to 200 backends based on its own view. A backend that just restarted has 0 connections. What tends to happen, and what algorithm mitigates it?

options.text: Nothing; least-connections handles this perfectly
options.explanation: Each proxy independently sees the restarted backend as the least loaded and sends it new traffic at the same time. Together they overwhelm it.

options.text: The backend is ignored until it reaches the average connection count
options.explanation: Least-connections does the opposite: a backend with the fewest connections is the most attractive target.

options.text: All 50 proxies simultaneously pick the empty backend (herding), overloading it; power of two choices limits this because each proxy only compares two random backends
options.explanation: Correct. With P2C, the empty backend wins only when it's one of the two sampled, so its share of new traffic rises gradually rather than all proxies piling on together.

options.text: Round robin would be worse, because it can't spread load
options.explanation: Round robin would actually not herd onto the restarted node (it'd get 1/200 of traffic), though it ignores load in other ways. The specific fix for herding with load awareness is P2C.

questions.workedExample:
1. Global least-connections: each proxy picks the backend with the fewest connections in its own view of the 200.
2. A freshly restarted backend has 0 connections, so it is the least loaded for **every** proxy at once.
3. All 50 proxies send it new requests until their local counts catch up, and their views lag, so it overloads, possibly into a crash loop.
4. **Power of two choices**: each request samples two backends at random and picks the less loaded. The fresh backend wins only when it is one of the two sampled, which happens for about 1 request in 100, roughly double its fair share of 1 in 200: a modest bump, not a pile-on.
5. Add a **slow start** ramp for new backends (gradually increasing their weight), as Envoy and HAProxy support, to cover warm-up too.

lessons.title: Hash affinity without a resize stampede
lessons.summary: Compare modulo hashing with a consistent-hash ring and virtual nodes.
lessons.body:
Cache affinity needs stable key ownership while the fleet changes. This is a different objective from sending every new request to whichever server is least busy.

### Hashing and consistent hashing

Sometimes you *want* the same key to go to the same server: for example, routing by user ID to a server that has that user's data cached.

Naive hashing sends each key to server number `hash(key) % N`: the remainder when the key's hash is divided by the number of servers `N`. That works until `N` changes. A key keeps its server only if dividing its hash by the old and the new server count leaves the same remainder, which happens for only about one key in `N + 1`.

So going from 10 to 11 servers remaps about **91%** (10 in 11) of keys. Every cache is effectively flushed at once, and the misses land on the database behind it: a stampede of misses caused by adding capacity.

**Consistent hashing** places servers and keys on a ring; each key goes to the next server clockwise:

```
        S1
     /      \
  k3          k1
  |            |
  S3          S2
     \      /
        k2
k1 -> S2, k2 -> S3, k3 -> S1
```

Adding or removing a server only moves the keys in its arc. On average a joining server takes over one share of the enlarged ring, so adding an 11th server to 10 moves about 9% (1 in 11) of keys instead of 91%. A leaving server hands over its former share.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Counting off into groups versus a round table
> A teacher splits a class into 10 groups by having pupils count off "1 to 10" along a line. Add an 11th group and recount, and almost everyone gets a new group. Now seat the pupils around a round table with the group helpers spaced among them, and each pupil joins the next helper clockwise. A new helper who sits down takes over only the pupils just before their seat.
>
> **How it maps:** counting off is `hash(key) % N`, so changing N changes nearly every key's server. The round table is the consistent-hash ring, the helpers are servers and the pupils are keys, so a join moves only one arc of keys.
>
> **Where it stops:** positions on the ring come from a hash, not from where anyone chooses to sit, and with virtual nodes each server occupies many scattered places at once so its share evens out. A key that moves also lands on a cold cache, a cost the seating picture leaves out.

Each server gets many **virtual nodes** on the ring (say 100–200) so the load evens out. Variants include **rendezvous (HRW) hashing** and Google's **Maglev hashing**, which fills a fixed-size table mapping hash values to backends for fast, near-even assignment with minimal disruption. Consistent hashing is covered in more depth in the partitioning lessons; here, its job is cache affinity.

### Choosing

| Workload | Good choice |
|---|---|
| Uniform, short requests | Round robin |
| Variable request cost | Least requests / P2C |
| Many LB instances | Power of two choices |
| Cache or session affinity | Consistent hashing |
| Mixed server sizes | Weighted variants |

With only one ring point per server, random gaps can be very unequal and one failed server’s whole arc goes to its clockwise neighbour. Virtual nodes give each physical server many scattered arcs, so total ownership averages out and a failure can spread keys among several neighbours.

## Key takeaways

- Changing the modulo server count remaps most keys, creating cold-cache load.
- A consistent-hash join moves mainly the new server’s share; a removal redistributes its former share.
- Many virtual nodes smooth ownership and scatter the destinations that inherit a failed server’s keys.

## Further reading

- [Maglev (Google Research)](https://research.google/pubs/maglev-a-fast-and-reliable-software-network-load-balancer/)
- [Consistent hashing (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consistent_hashing)

questions.prompt: You route requests to 10 cache servers using `hash(user_id) % N`, where N is the number of servers. You add an 11th server during a traffic peak. Predict what happens next.

options.text: Nearly every user (about 10 in 11) maps to a different server, so the caches are effectively flushed and the database behind them takes a surge of misses
options.explanation: Correct. A key keeps its server only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 10 and for 11, which is true for about 1 key in 11. Adding capacity this way causes a cold-cache stampede.

options.text: Only about 1 user in 11 moves, to the new server, so caches stay mostly warm
options.explanation: That is what consistent hashing achieves. With modulo hashing, every key's server is recomputed with the new N, and most change.

options.text: About half the users move
options.explanation: There is no reason for half. For a key to stay, its remainders for 10 and 11 must match, which is rare, so far more than half move.

options.text: No users move, because existing keys keep their servers until they expire
options.explanation: Modulo hashing has no memory of earlier placements: the next request for every key is routed using the new N.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under `hash % N`, a key stays put only if dividing its hash by 10 and by 11 leaves the same remainder.
2. Across a full cycle of hash values, that happens for only about 1 in 11 of them, so roughly 10 in 11 keys (about 91%) move.
3. Each moved key now looks for its data on a server that has never cached it: a miss that falls through to the database. Doing this at peak can overload the database.
4. With consistent hashing (and virtual nodes), the new server takes over only about 1/11 of the ring, so only about 9% of keys move, all of them to the new server.

That difference decides whether adding capacity relieves load or triggers a stampede.

questions.prompt: You use consistent hashing with **one** point per server for 4 cache servers. One server ends up owning 45% of the ring and another only 8%. When that busy server fails, all its keys move to a single neighbour. What fixes both problems?

options.text: Switch to `hash(key) % 4`
options.explanation: Modulo hashing spreads keys evenly, but adding or removing a server remaps almost every key, which is the problem consistent hashing solves.

options.text: Use a stronger hash function such as SHA-256
options.explanation: Even a perfect hash places 4 random points unevenly on the ring; with so few points, arc sizes vary wildly. Better randomness doesn't fix small numbers.

options.text: Give each server many virtual nodes (say 100–200 points) on the ring
options.explanation: Correct. With many points per server, each server's total arc averages out close to 25%, and a failed server's arcs are scattered, so its keys spread across all survivors instead of one neighbour.

options.text: Make every key go to the two nearest servers
options.explanation: Replication improves availability, but it doesn't even out arc sizes or stop one neighbour inheriting all of a failed server's load.

questions.workedExample:
1. With 4 random points, the 4 gaps between them are very uneven: 45% versus 8% is a possible illustrative outcome, rather than a guaranteed distribution.
2. Each server owns the arc before its point → uneven load.
3. On failure, its single arc merges into its clockwise neighbour → one server takes all the load.
4. With 150 virtual nodes per server: 600 points; each server owns 150 small arcs → totals close to 25% each.
5. On failure, its 150 small arcs go to many different neighbours → load spreads roughly evenly over 3 survivors.

lessons.title: Detection delay and health policy
lessons.summary: Predict how long a dead backend keeps receiving traffic, and choose checks and fail-open behaviour deliberately.
lessons.body:
A balancer’s availability claim depends on what it measures and what it does when healthy capacity disappears. Separate the detection model from the policy used after detection.

## Health checks

A balancer must know which backends can take traffic.

- **Active checks:** the balancer probes each backend, e.g. `GET /healthz` every 5–10 s. Mark a backend unhealthy after a set number of consecutive failures (the *unhealthy threshold*, say 2–3), and healthy again after a set number of consecutive successes (the *healthy threshold*).
- **Passive checks (outlier detection):** watch real traffic; eject a backend that returns, say, 5 consecutive 5xx errors (Envoy's default) or times out, for a cool-off period.

Active checks can discover a dead server independently of user traffic, but requests may still fail before the next checks detect it; passive checks catch servers that answer `/healthz` happily but fail real requests. Use both.

Active checks also leave a detection window. If a server dies just after passing a probe, the balancer needs several more failed probes before it acts, so the window is roughly the probe interval multiplied by the unhealthy threshold (plus probe timeouts). With a 10 s interval and a threshold of 3, a dead server can keep receiving its share of traffic for about 30 s, and every request sent to it in that time fails unless something retries it elsewhere. Shorter intervals shrink the window at the cost of more probe traffic; passive outlier detection and retries of idempotent requests reduce the damage without waiting for probes.

What should `/healthz` check? This is where teams get burned:

- **Too shallow** (just "process is up"): a server whose database pool is exhausted keeps getting traffic and returning errors.
- **Too deep** (checks the database, cache and three downstream services): when the shared database blips, *every* backend fails its health check at once, the balancer removes them all, and a partial outage becomes a total one.

> [!warning] Fail open
> A configurable availability trade-off: if too many backends are unhealthy, some balancers route to all of them anyway. This can help when checks are misleading or healthy capacity is insufficient, but it can also send traffic to truly broken hosts; disable fail-open where serving such responses is unacceptable. Envoy calls this the *panic threshold* (default 50%). Whether partial service is preferable to rejection depends on the workload and the kinds of errors it could return. Similarly, separate **liveness probes** ("restart me") from **readiness probes** ("don't send me traffic right now"), as Kubernetes does.

## Key takeaways

- Combine active probes with passive outlier detection; neither observes every failure immediately.
- Probe interval times failure threshold sets the rough worst-case window in which a dead backend still gets traffic.
- Deep shared-dependency checks can remove every backend; fail-open and readiness policies need explicit decisions.

## Further reading

- [Target group health checks (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)
- [Panic threshold (Envoy)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/panic_threshold)

questions.prompt: Every app server health check queries the shared primary database. During a 20-second database failover, the balancer marks a backend unhealthy after two probes 5 seconds apart and is configured to fail closed when all are unhealthy. What can happen, and how can the design improve?

options.text: Nothing bad; the balancer just waits for the database
options.explanation: The balancer doesn't know about the database. It sees every backend failing its health check and removes them all.

options.text: Only one backend fails, so traffic moves to the others
options.explanation: All backends share the same database, so they all fail the same check at the same moment. There's nowhere to move traffic to.

options.text: The balancer automatically switches to the database replica
options.explanation: Load balancers in front of app servers don't manage database connections; failing over the database is a separate mechanism.

options.text: All backends can be marked unhealthy together, so this fail-closed balancer also rejects database-independent requests. Separate shared-dependency handling from readiness and choose fail-open policy deliberately.
options.explanation: Correct. A deep dependency check turns a shared-dependency blip into a total outage. Check local health (process, thread pool, ability to respond) for readiness, handle dependency failures per request, and rely on fail-open or panic thresholds as a safety net.

questions.workedExample:
1. The shared database is unavailable for 20 seconds. The stated 5-second/two-failure checks can mark all app servers unhealthy before recovery.
2. This fail-closed balancer then rejects even requests that do not use the database.
3. Recovery checks can prolong the visible outage.
4. Design readiness around the traffic each instance can actually serve, handle dependency failures per request, and explicitly choose fail-open versus fail-closed.
5. Product behavior differs: AWS ALB fails open when all registered targets are unhealthy; Envoy has a configurable panic threshold.

questions.prompt: An active checker probes each backend every 10 seconds and marks it unhealthy after three consecutive failures. One backend, receiving 200 requests per second, crashes just after a passing check. With no retries or passive checks, its share of traffic keeps failing for roughly 30 seconds, thousands of requests. Which change most directly cuts the number of failed user requests without tripling probe traffic?

options.text: Raise the healthy threshold so recovered backends return more slowly
options.explanation: The healthy threshold controls how a backend *returns* to service. It does nothing to detect this crash sooner.

options.text: Add passive outlier detection on real traffic, and let the balancer retry idempotent requests on another backend
options.explanation: Correct. Passive checks notice consecutive connection failures or 5xx responses from real requests without waiting for the next probes, and retries of idempotent requests turn many of the remaining failures into successes elsewhere.

options.text: Raise the unhealthy threshold to five failures to avoid false alarms
options.explanation: A higher threshold lengthens the detection window (roughly interval times threshold), so more requests fail before removal.

options.text: Make `/healthz` query the database and every downstream service
options.explanation: A deeper check does not run more often, so it detects this crash no faster, and it risks marking every backend unhealthy when a shared dependency blips.

questions.workedExample:
1. The detection window for active checks is roughly the probe interval multiplied by the unhealthy threshold: about 30 s here, because the crash happened just after a pass.
2. Every request the balancer sends to the dead backend in that window fails, so the number of failures grows with both the window and that backend's request rate.
3. Two levers cut it without more probes:
  - **Passive outlier detection** watches real responses and can eject the backend after a few consecutive failures; connection or request timeouts can still delay that signal.
  - **Retries** of idempotent requests on another backend rescue many requests that hit the dead one.
4. Shorter probe intervals also shrink the window, but at the cost of more probe traffic. Raising thresholds or deepening checks makes things worse.

link.title: Health checks for target groups (AWS ALB)

questions.prompt: An Envoy cluster has one priority, ten equally weighted backends, no degraded or excluded hosts, and default fail-open panic behavior. Six fail health checks and four are healthy; the panic threshold is 50%. How does it route?

options.text: Only to the 4 healthy backends
options.explanation: That's what happens while at least 50% of hosts are healthy. Here only 40% are, which is below the threshold.

options.text: It returns 503 to every request until more backends recover
options.explanation: Panic mode exists to avoid exactly that. Envoy keeps serving rather than failing everything.

options.text: It sends all traffic to a single backend
options.explanation: Nothing in Envoy's behaviour concentrates traffic on one host in this situation.

options.text: Across all 10 backends, ignoring health status, because healthy hosts (40%) are below the 50% panic threshold
options.explanation: Correct. Envoy assumes that when most hosts look unhealthy, the health checks themselves may be wrong, or the healthy few would be overwhelmed. Some requests fail, but roughly 40% succeed instead of risking a total collapse.

questions.workedExample:
1. Only 4 of 10 hosts (40%) are healthy, which is below Envoy's default 50% panic threshold.
2. In panic mode, Envoy balances across **all** hosts as if they were healthy.
3. Likely outcome: roughly 40% of requests reach good hosts and succeed, instead of four hosts receiving all the load and possibly falling over too.
4. Trade-off: if the six really are dead, you serve some errors; if the checks are wrong (for example a shared-dependency blip), you avoid a self-inflicted outage.

lessons.title: Session affinity and graceful draining
lessons.summary: Keep deploys and scaling from trapping sessions or synchronising client reconnects.
lessons.body:
Scaling and deployments change which servers exist. Keeping session correctness independent of a particular backend and moving long-lived clients gradually makes those changes easier to absorb.

### Graceful draining

When removing a server (deploy, scale-in), stop sending it **new** requests but let in-flight ones finish: AWS calls this *deregistration delay* (default 300 s). Without it, deploys cause bursts of reset connections.

## Sticky sessions

**Session affinity** routes a client's requests to the same backend, typically via a cookie the balancer sets (e.g. `AWSALB`) or by hashing the client IP.

It's useful when servers hold per-user state in memory: a legacy session store, a WebSocket connection, a warm cache. But it costs you:

- **Uneven load.** A few heavy users can pin one server hot.
- **Fragile failover.** When the server dies, its users lose their sessions.
- **Slower scaling.** New servers only get *new* users; existing ones stay put.
- **IP hashing breaks behind NAT:** a whole office or mobile carrier can map to one server.

The usual better answer is to make servers **stateless** and keep session data in a shared store (Redis, a database) or a signed token, so any server can handle any request. Use stickiness for cache affinity, not correctness.

## The balancer itself must not be a single point of failure

- Run balancers in pairs or fleets: active/passive with a floating IP (keepalived/VRRP), or active/active behind ECMP or anycast.
- Managed balancer resilience depends on the product and configured zones; configure the supported multi-zone topology and place backends across failure domains.
- Watch for **connection limits and warm-up**: some managed balancers scale gradually, so a sudden 10× spike (a launch, a television advert) can outrun them. Pre-warming or load testing helps.

A WebSocket can outlive the entire drain window. Do not wait for thousands of such connections to reach the same removal deadline: close them gradually during the window and make clients reconnect with exponential backoff and random jitter. Spreading server closes and client retries prevents a synchronised reconnect spike; the suitable batch size and window depend on spare fleet capacity.

## Key takeaways

- Stickiness can preserve local state but creates uneven load, fragile failover and slower scaling.
- Drain new work away and let existing work finish; long-lived sockets need an explicit reconnect plan.
- Run resilient balancer topology and test connection limits and sudden load growth.

## Further reading

- [Sticky sessions (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/sticky-sessions.html)
- [Deregistration delay and target attributes (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html)
- [Retry with backoff pattern (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/retry-backoff.html)

questions.prompt: Your app stores user sessions in server memory and relies on sticky sessions at the load balancer. Which problems should you expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: When a server crashes, its users lose their sessions and get logged out
options.explanation: Correct. The session data only existed in that server's memory; affinity can't move it elsewhere.

options.text: Newly added servers take a long time to share the load, because existing users stay pinned
options.explanation: Correct. Only new sessions go to new servers. Scale-out during a spike barely helps the already-hot servers.

options.text: Load can become uneven if some pinned users are much heavier than others
options.explanation: Correct. Affinity overrides the balancing algorithm; a server with a few heavy users can't shed them.

options.text: TLS stops working with sticky sessions
options.explanation: Stickiness is implemented with cookies or hashing at the L7 balancer, which terminates TLS anyway. It has no effect on TLS.

options.text: If affinity is by client IP, users behind one carrier NAT all land on the same server
options.explanation: Correct. Thousands of mobile users can share a few public IPs, so IP-hash stickiness concentrates them.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through the life of a sticky session:

1. **Placement** fixed at first request → no rebalancing later (uneven load, slow scale-out).
2. **State** lives only on that server → lost on crash or deploy.
3. **Key choice**: cookies are per browser; IP hash is per NAT gateway → hot spots.

Fix: move session state to Redis or a signed token, so any server can serve any request; keep stickiness only as a cache-locality optimisation.

questions.prompt: Your chat service holds WebSocket connections that last for hours behind an ALB with a 300 s deregistration delay. On every deploy, about 50,000 clients disconnect within the same second and then reconnect at once, causing a load spike and failed logins. What's the best improvement?

options.text: Raise the deregistration delay to 24 hours
options.explanation: A 24-hour value is outside the ALB deregistration-delay range (0–3,600 seconds). Even a longer supported delay does not itself spread reconnects.

options.text: Disable health checks during deploys
options.explanation: Health checks don't cause the disconnects; draining does. Turning them off risks sending traffic to broken instances.

options.text: Switch to round-robin balancing
options.explanation: The algorithm chooses where new connections go; it doesn't change the fact that 50,000 clients reconnect at the same moment.

options.text: Have draining servers close their WebSockets gradually over the drain window, and make clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus random jitter
options.explanation: Correct. Spreading closes over the window and jittering client reconnects turn a 50,000-in-one-second spike into a steady trickle that the fleet absorbs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Draining lets in-flight work finish, but a WebSocket is never "finished"; at the end of the delay the balancer cuts everything still open.
2. All of a server's clients drop together, so they all reconnect together: a **thundering herd**.
3. Server side: on drain, close connections in batches spread across most of the window, with a "please reconnect" close code.
4. Client side: before each reconnect attempt, wait a random delay whose upper limit grows with each failed attempt (exponential backoff with full jitter).
5. Result: spreading 50,000 closes over a few minutes means a few hundred reconnects per second instead of 50,000 in one second, a rate the fleet can absorb.

lessons.title: Proxy buffering and trusted client addresses
lessons.summary: Distinguish proxy direction, decouple slow clients and validate forwarded address chains.
lessons.body:
Reverse proxies, API gateways and service meshes are often built from the same software (Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy) and share many features. The difference is mostly **where they sit** and **whose problems they solve**:

- A **reverse proxy** fronts a set of servers.
- An **API gateway** fronts a set of *APIs* for external clients.
- A **service mesh** handles traffic *between* your services.

```
         Internet
            |
     [CDN / edge proxy]
            |
      [API gateway]      <- north-south
            |
   +--------+--------+
   |                 |
[svc A]+sidecar  [svc B]+sidecar
   |     <---- mesh ---->  |
   |   (east-west, mTLS)   |
```

"North-south" traffic enters and leaves your system; "east-west" traffic flows between services inside it.

## Forward vs reverse proxy

A **forward proxy** acts for *clients*: a corporate proxy that all employees' browsers go through. The server sees the proxy, not the user.

A **reverse proxy** acts for *servers*: clients think they're talking to `example.com`, but they're talking to a proxy that forwards to hidden backends.

## Reverse proxies

A reverse proxy (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik) typically handles:

| Job | Why at the proxy |
|---|---|
| TLS termination | One place for certs |
| Load balancing | Hide backend topology |
| Compression | Offload CPU from apps |
| Static files, caching | Fast, no app involved |
| Buffering | Protect slow apps |
| Request limits | Size, timeouts, rate |

**Buffering** deserves a mention. A slow mobile client might take 10 s to upload a request or download a response. If an app server process (say a Python worker) talked to it directly, that worker would be stuck for 10 s. With request/response buffering enabled and enough buffer or temporary-file capacity, NGINX can decouple a synchronous worker from a slow client. The worker remains busy for response generation and transfer to the proxy, not necessarily only milliseconds. Streaming, buffer limits and disabled buffering change this behavior. This is why NGINX in front of Gunicorn or Puma is standard practice.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A waiter between the kitchen and slow diners
> A restaurant has a few skilled chefs. If each chef had to carry every plate to the table and wait while the diner chatted before returning, most of their time would be spent standing in the dining room. Instead, the chef hands the finished plate to a waiter at the pass and starts the next dish; waiters, who are cheap to add, deal with slow diners.
>
> **How it maps:** the chefs are the expensive synchronous app workers, the waiter is the proxy's event loop holding many slow client connections, and the pass is the proxy's buffer. Handing over the finished response lets the worker serve the next request.
>
> **Where it stops:** the hand-off only works if the proxy has enough buffer or temporary-file space, and it does not apply to streamed responses, which must flow through as they are produced. Unlike a waiter, the proxy can also buffer the incoming request body so the worker doesn't wait for a slow upload.

The proxy also adds headers so the app knows the real client: `X-Forwarded-For` (client IP), `X-Forwarded-Proto` (was it HTTPS?) and the standardised `Forwarded` header (RFC 7239). Each proxy *appends* the address it received the connection from, so after a CDN and a load balancer the header reads `client, CDN`, and the app sees the load balancer as the connection's source address.

> [!warning] Trusting forwarded headers
> Clients can send their own `X-Forwarded-For`. First verify that the direct peer is a trusted proxy, then parse the forwarded chain from the right, skipping only explicitly trusted proxy hops. The first untrusted address is the client boundary; it may itself be an external proxy, not the original person’s device. Ensure attackers cannot bypass the trusted entry path. Otherwise attackers can spoof their IP to bypass rate limits or IP allow-lists.

### Streaming changes the buffering choice

For Server-Sent Events, buffering small updates can delay their arrival and produce bursts. NGINX can disable response buffering for the streaming route with `proxy_buffering off;` or, when permitted by its configuration, the response header `X-Accel-Buffering: no`. These are illustrative directive and header fragments, not a complete server configuration. Check read timeouts and send stream keep-alives as appropriate; changing buffering does not make synchronous application workers asynchronous.

## Key takeaways

- A forward proxy represents clients; a reverse proxy represents backend servers.
- Buffering can free synchronous workers, but streaming routes need different buffering decisions.
- Verify the direct trusted peer and walk forwarded addresses from the right; client-supplied headers can be forged.

## Further reading

- [Proxy buffering (NGINX)](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_buffering)
- [X-Forwarded-For (MDN)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/X-Forwarded-For)
- [Forwarded HTTP extension (RFC 7239)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7239)

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a forward proxy from a reverse proxy?

options.text: A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients (servers see the proxy); a reverse proxy acts on behalf of servers (clients see the proxy)
options.explanation: Correct. A corporate web proxy hides users from websites; NGINX in front of your app hides backends from users.

options.text: A forward proxy only handles HTTP; a reverse proxy only handles TCP
options.explanation: Both kinds can handle HTTP, and both can work at the TCP level. Protocol isn't what separates them; whose side they're on is.

options.text: A reverse proxy sends responses backwards to the server
options.explanation: 'Reverse' refers to the direction of representation (it stands in for servers), not to the direction data flows.

options.text: They're the same thing with different names
options.explanation: They're deployed by different parties for different reasons: one by the client's network, one by the service operator.

questions.workedExample:
Ask: **who deploys it, and who is hidden?**

| | Deployed by | Hides |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | Client's org | Clients |
| Reverse | Service owner | Servers |

Examples: Squid at a company or school (forward); NGINX, HAProxy or a CDN in front of a website (reverse).

questions.prompt: A server has 8 synchronous workers. Assume an unbuffered slow response occupies a worker for 5 s, while enabled NGINX buffering with adequate capacity lets the worker finish generation and transfer in 50 ms. Why can buffering raise the worker-limited throughput?

options.text: NGINX makes the mobile network faster
options.explanation: NGINX can't change the client's network speed. The slow download still takes 5 s; it just no longer ties up a Python worker.

options.text: NGINX caches every response so the app never runs
options.explanation: NGINX can cache, but personalised responses usually aren't cached. The throughput gain here comes from buffering, which works for uncacheable responses too.

options.text: NGINX buffers the response, freeing the Python worker in milliseconds while NGINX's event loop handles the slow client
options.explanation: Correct. NGINX handles thousands of slow connections cheaply in one event loop, so the 8 expensive workers spend their time generating responses rather than waiting on sockets.

options.text: NGINX converts the app to async Python
options.explanation: A proxy can't change how the app is written. It isolates the app from slow clients instead.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each synchronous worker handles one request at a time, so the most the server can complete is limited by how long each request occupies a worker.
2. Unbuffered, a worker is stuck for the whole slow download (5 s here), so 8 workers complete very few requests per second.
3. With buffering, NGINX takes the whole response into its buffer in about 50 ms and feeds the slow client from its event loop, which handles thousands of slow connections cheaply. The worker is free to start the next request.
4. Freeing each worker about 100 times sooner raises this ideal worker-limited ceiling by about 100 times.

This is not a benchmark of overall throughput. Client bandwidth, proxy memory or disk buffers, CPU and connection limits can become the next bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Your rate limiter keys on the first IP in `X-Forwarded-For`. Attackers bypass it easily. Why?

options.text: `X-Forwarded-For` is encrypted, so the limiter reads garbage
options.explanation: It's a plain HTTP header, readable by any hop that terminates TLS. The problem is trust, not encryption.

options.text: Clients can send their own `X-Forwarded-For`; proxies append to it, so the left-most value is attacker-controlled. Use the entry added by your own trusted proxy.
options.explanation: Correct. An attacker sends `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` with a random IP each time; your proxy appends the real IP at the end. Read from the right, skipping known proxies.

options.text: IP addresses can't be used for rate limiting
options.explanation: IP-based limits are common and useful (with caveats about NAT). They only fail here because the IP is being read from a spoofable position.

options.text: The load balancer strips the header
options.explanation: If it were stripped, the limiter would see nothing at all, not attacker-chosen values. The symptom points to trusting client-supplied data.

questions.workedExample:
1. Attacker sends: `X-Forwarded-For: 9.9.9.9` (random each request).
2. Your CDN appends the real client IP: `9.9.9.9, 203.0.113.5`.
3. Your LB appends the CDN's IP: `9.9.9.9, 203.0.113.5, 198.51.100.7`.
4. Taking the **first** entry gives `9.9.9.9`: attacker-chosen.
5. Correct: walk from the **right**, discard addresses of hops you trust (LB, CDN ranges); the first untrusted one, `203.0.113.5`, is the real client.

questions.prompt: You add a Server-Sent Events endpoint that streams small price updates every second. Behind NGINX, clients receive nothing for a while and then a burst of many updates at once. What's the likely cause and fix?

options.text: SSE doesn't work over HTTPS
options.explanation: SSE works fine over HTTPS; the symptom is about batching, not failure.

options.text: The browser is caching the stream
options.explanation: Browsers don't cache an open event stream; they process events as they arrive.

options.text: NGINX's response buffering collects the stream's output until a buffer fills or the response ends; disable buffering for that route (for example `proxy_buffering off`, or the app sending `X-Accel-Buffering: no`)
options.explanation: Correct as a likely buffering diagnosis. Disable response buffering for this route so NGINX passes bytes through as received; the X-Accel-Buffering header works only if configuration permits it. Also verify that the application flushes events and that compression or another intermediary is not buffering them.

options.text: The app server needs more worker processes
options.explanation: More workers wouldn't change how NGINX batches the stream's bytes before sending them on.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal case: NGINX reads the app's response into buffers so a slow client can't hold up a worker. Great for ordinary pages.
2. Streaming case: each event is a few hundred bytes; buffering can delay small updates and produce bursts; there is no universal rule that NGINX flushes only a full buffer.
3. Fix per route: `proxy_buffering off;` in that `location`, or have the app send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` when NGINX has not disabled that header’s effect.
4. Also check proxy read timeouts, which can cut long-lived streams, and send periodic keep-alive comments.

Buffering is a trade-off: useful for many ordinary responses, but low-latency event streams usually need immediate forwarding and application flushing.

lessons.title: API policy and backends for frontends
lessons.summary: Centralise external API policy and move chatty client calls onto the service network.
lessons.body:
External clients need a stable API even when many internal services implement it. A gateway handles shared API policy; a backend for frontend adapts the service calls and response to one client experience.

## API gateways

An API gateway is a reverse proxy specialised for **APIs consumed by external clients**. Products include AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee, Azure API Management, and Envoy-based gateways.

On top of reverse-proxy features, it adds **API-level concerns**:

- **Authentication and authorisation:** validate JWTs, OAuth tokens or API keys once, at the front door, and pass the identity downstream.
- **Rate limiting and quotas** per API key or customer ("1,000 requests per minute on the free plan").
- **Routing to many services:** `/orders` → order service, `/users` → user service, so clients see one API.
- **Request/response transformation:** protocol translation (REST to gRPC), versioning, field filtering.
- **Developer-facing features:** API keys, usage analytics, billing, documentation portals.

### Backends for frontends

The **BFF** pattern uses a separate gateway (or thin service) per client type: one for the mobile app, one for the web app. Each aggregates and shapes data for its client, for example combining five service calls into one response so a phone on a slow network makes one round trip instead of five.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A reception desk and a personal assistant
> Every visitor to a large office passes one reception desk, which checks identification, signs them in, enforces visiting rules and tells them where to go. A busy executive might instead send a personal assistant, who visits five departments in the building and comes back with one folder.
>
> **How it maps:** reception is the API gateway: one front door applying shared policy (authentication, quotas, routing) before requests reach the services. The assistant is a backend for frontend, making several dependent internal calls on the client's behalf so the slow outside trip happens once.
>
> **Where it stops:** reception checks a visitor once at the door, but a gateway checks every single request, so when it is slow or down every API suffers. A BFF serves every user of one kind of client (all phone users, say), not one person. And unlike a trusted receptionist's badge, passing the gateway does not settle access: each service must still check whether this caller may see this particular resource.

### Gateway pitfalls

- **Business logic creep.** Gateways become a dumping ground for logic that belongs in services, creating a fragile, centrally owned bottleneck. Keep them about *cross-cutting* concerns.
- **Single point of failure.** All external traffic flows through it; it needs redundancy across zones and careful change management.
- **Added latency.** Each hop adds work and can add latency; the amount depends on topology, load, buffering, protocol and enabled plug-ins.

## Key takeaways

- A gateway is a natural place for external authentication, customer quotas and API routing.
- A BFF shapes one response for its client type and moves dependent calls onto the backend network.
- Keep business logic in services and make the gateway resilient; its extra processing also has a cost.

## Further reading

- [API gateway and BFF pattern (microservices.io)](https://microservices.io/patterns/apigateway.html)
- [What is Amazon API Gateway?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: Your public API has free and paid tiers: 100 and 10,000 requests per minute per API key. Requests must be authenticated with OAuth tokens before reaching any of your 12 services. Where is the most natural place to enforce this?

options.text: In each of the 12 services' code
options.explanation: That duplicates auth and quota logic 12 times, possibly in several languages, and makes per-key quotas across services hard to count consistently.

options.text: In the service mesh sidecars
options.explanation: Meshes focus on service-to-service (east-west) traffic: mTLS identity between services. Customer API keys and commercial quotas belong at the external entry point.

options.text: In DNS
options.explanation: DNS only maps names to addresses; it never sees tokens or individual requests, so it can't authenticate or count them.

options.text: In an API gateway at the edge of the system
options.explanation: Correct. Authenticating tokens and enforcing per-key quotas are classic north-south, cross-cutting API concerns. The gateway does them once and forwards the verified identity downstream.

questions.workedExample:
1. Who's the concern for? **External API consumers** → north-south → gateway.
2. Is it cross-cutting? Yes: every endpoint needs auth and quotas.
3. Gateway flow: validate OAuth token → look up the key's plan → check counter (e.g. in Redis) → forward with `X-User-Id` or a signed internal token.
4. Services still enforce **authorisation** on their own resources ("can this user see order 42?") because that's business logic.

questions.prompt: Your mobile app's home screen calls 6 back-end services one after another, because each call needs data from the previous one. Phones are about 150 ms RTT from your region, and services are about 1 ms from each other inside it. The team proposes a backend for frontend (BFF) that makes those 6 calls server-side. Which prediction is right?

options.text: Network time drops from about six slow phone round trips to about one, because the six dependent calls now run over the fast internal network
options.explanation: Correct. The phone makes one round trip to the BFF, and the six sequential calls each cost about 1 ms inside the region instead of 150 ms over the mobile path. Most of the screen's network wait disappears.

options.text: Only the few milliseconds of internal latency are saved
options.explanation: The saving comes from replacing five slow phone round trips with fast internal calls, not from shaving the internal hops.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the same 6 calls are still made
options.explanation: The calls still happen, but over a 1 ms network instead of a 150 ms one. Where a round trip happens matters as much as how many there are.

options.text: All network time disappears, because the BFF runs next to the services
options.explanation: The phone still needs one round trip to reach the BFF, so one slow trip remains.

questions.workedExample:
| Design | Slow phone round trips | Fast internal calls |
|---|---|---|
| App calls 6 services | 6 | 0 |
| App → BFF → 6 services | 1 | 6 |

1. The calls are sequential, so each one waits for the previous answer: six slow trips in a row is the worst case.
2. A BFF keeps the dependency chain but moves it inside the region, where each hop costs about a millisecond.
3. The phone pays a single slow round trip and receives one response shaped for the screen.

A BFF, an aggregating gateway or GraphQL all move chatty, dependent calls onto the fast internal network.

lessons.title: Mesh planes, sidecars and ambient mode
lessons.summary: Explain mesh traffic features, trace-context limits and the costs of sidecar or ambient deployment.
lessons.body:
A mesh provides networking policy between services. Compare it with libraries and gateways by the traffic it controls, then budget the resource and operational cost of the chosen data plane.

## Service meshes

Inside a microservice system, every service needs the same networking features: retries, timeouts, load balancing, mTLS, metrics and tracing. You can put these in a **library** in each service (Netflix's Hystrix and Ribbon era, or today's gRPC client libraries), but then every language needs its own implementation, and upgrades mean redeploying every service.

A **service mesh** moves them into the infrastructure:

```
[ App A ]          [ App B ]
    |                  ^
    v                  |
[proxy A] ==mTLS==> [proxy B]
    ^                  ^
    |  config, certs   |
    +--[control plane]-+
```

- **Data plane in classic sidecar mode:** a proxy next to each enrolled service instance intercepts configured inbound and outbound traffic; exclusions and unsupported protocols need separate consideration.
- **Control plane:** (Istio's `istiod`, Linkerd's control plane) distributes routing rules, certificates and policies to every proxy.

What you get, without changing app code:

1. **mTLS for enrolled and configured traffic**, with automatic certificate issuance and rotation, plus service identity (e.g. SPIFFE IDs) for authorisation policies like "only `checkout` may call `payments`".
2. **Traffic management:** retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, outlier ejection, and per-request L7 load balancing (which fixes the long-lived HTTP/2 connection imbalance).
3. **Progressive delivery:** send 5% of traffic to `v2`, or route by header for testing.
4. **Uniform observability:** request rates, error rates and latency for service pairs, and proxy tracing spans. End-to-end trace linkage still requires the application to propagate incoming trace context into outgoing calls.

### The costs

- **Latency:** a classic two-sidecar call adds client and server proxy processing; measure its median and tail overhead under your actual load.
- **Resources:** a sidecar per pod, each with its own CPU and memory; across thousands of pods this adds up.
- **Operational complexity:** the control plane is now critical infrastructure. A bad config push can break every service at once.
- **Debugging:** "is it my app or the mesh?" becomes a common question.

> [!note] Measurement gap
> No reproducible gateway or mesh benchmark is supplied here. Fixed per-hop latency and universal per-client memory/capacity estimates are omitted.

Newer designs reduce the overhead: Istio's **ambient mode** replaces per-pod sidecars with a per-node L4 proxy (ztunnel) plus optional shared L7 "waypoint" proxies, and **proxyless gRPC** has the gRPC library receive mesh config directly.

> [!tip] When to adopt a mesh
> A mesh pays off when you have **many services, several languages, and a real need** for mTLS, fine-grained traffic control or uniform telemetry. With five services in one language, a good shared client library and a gateway are usually simpler.

## Comparing the three

| | Reverse proxy | API gateway | Service mesh |
|---|---|---|---|
| Traffic | Into a service | Into the system | Between services |
| Main users | Ops | API consumers | Service teams |
| Typical jobs | TLS, LB, cache | Auth, quotas | mTLS, retries |
| Deployed as | A tier | A tier | Sidecar per pod |

In practice they combine: a CDN at the edge, an API gateway for external APIs (often itself an Envoy deployment, sometimes the mesh's own *ingress gateway*), and a mesh inside.

## Key takeaways

- The data plane handles enrolled traffic; the control plane distributes certificates, policy and routing.
- L7 retries, routing and telemetry depend on supported visible protocols; end-to-end traces need application context propagation.
- Ambient mode separates per-node L4 transport from optional L7 waypoints; adoption still needs an operational case.

## Further reading

- [What is Istio?](https://istio.io/latest/docs/concepts/what-is-istio/)
- [Ambient mode overview (Istio)](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ambient/overview/)
- [What is a service mesh? (Linkerd)](https://linkerd.io/what-is-a-service-mesh/)

questions.prompt: For traffic enrolled in a configured L7-capable mesh with supported HTTP protocols and no app-level TLS hiding requests from it, which features can the mesh provide without changing application code? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mutual TLS between services, with automatic certificate rotation
options.explanation: Correct. Sidecars handle the TLS handshakes using certificates issued and rotated by the control plane.

options.text: Per-request load balancing and retries with timeouts
options.explanation: Correct. The client-side sidecar balances each request across endpoints and applies retry and timeout policies from config.

options.text: Sending 5% of traffic to a new version
options.explanation: Correct. Weighted routing rules in the proxies split traffic between versions for canaries.

options.text: Fixing N+1 query problems in the database layer
options.explanation: A mesh sees network calls between services, not how an app queries its database. Query patterns are application logic.

options.text: Request-level metrics (rate, errors, latency) for each service pair
options.explanation: Correct. Since every call goes through proxies, they emit uniform golden-signal metrics. (Full distributed traces still need apps to propagate trace headers.)

questions.workedExample:
Ask, for each feature: **can a proxy beside the app do it just by seeing network traffic?**

- mTLS → yes, the proxy owns the connection.
- LB, retries, timeouts → yes, per request.
- Traffic splitting → yes, routing rules.
- Metrics → yes, it sees every request and response.
- Database query design → no, that's inside the app.
